# Agent 9 — CI/CD, GitHub Actions & Release Engineering Audit

Scope: `.github/workflows/*`, `.github/dependabot.yml`, `.github/zizmor.yml`,
`.github/scripts/{summary.py,prod-igy.js}`, `.pre-commit-config.yaml`,
`Makefile`, `Dockerfile`, `.dockerignore`, `action.yml`, `scripts/{bump_version,
check_version, check_workflow_summaries, commit_release_via_api,
version_surfaces}.py` and their tests. Read-only: no workflow was triggered, no
repo state was changed, no file outside this report was written.

## Summary

The pipeline is unusually well-documented (every workflow carries inline
history of the incident that shaped it) and the release automation
(`publish.yml`) has clearly been hardened twice already — once for the
unsigned-commit/admin-bypass incident, once for the "MERGED is not proof of
green" re-check. Run history over the last 100 runs is mostly green; the only
real failures are legitimate (`Dependency Review` catching real vulnerable
packages, two solo Dependabot update PRs that failed on `certifi`/`filelock`).

The two systemic problems are:

1. **The branch-protection ruleset and the workflow YAML have already drifted
   once, silently.** The required-status-checks list on `main`
   (`default-branch-protection`, ruleset 22778968) enumerates Python
   3.11/3.12/3.13 for each OS but **not 3.14**, and does not require the
   `container` (Docker) job at all, even though both exist in `ci.yml` and gate
   nothing is said about a reason to exclude them. A red 3.14 cell or a broken
   Dockerfile can merge to `main` today.
2. **The project ships (per its own README/CHANGELOG) to PyPI, npm, a GitHub
   Action, a VS Code extension, and "Docker" — but `publish.yml` only publishes
   to PyPI, the MCP Registry and npm.** There is no Docker image push to any
   registry anywhere in `.github/workflows/`, and no VS Code Marketplace /
   open-vsx publish step anywhere in the repo. `ci.yml`'s `container` job only
   builds and smoke-tests the image locally to the runner; it is never pushed.
   If a published Docker image or VS Code extension exists, it is not produced
   by anything in this repository's CI.

Beyond that, quality gates (ruff, ruff format, mypy, pytest, coverage) are
genuinely enforced on every PR with no `continue-on-error` disguising a
failure, the Python-3.10 drop was applied consistently (no workflow still
installs or tests 3.10), and the release pipeline's idempotency (tag
re-use checks, `skip-existing`, npm/mcp-publisher "already published" guards)
is well thought through. The two live gaps that most need attention are the
required-checks/matrix drift above and the fact that `enforce_admins` is
still off and ruleset bypass is still granted to `RepositoryRole 5` — i.e. the
exact mechanism that let 3.0.0 ship on a red test suite is still live,
mitigated now only by `publish.yml`'s own in-run re-check of required checks
(added after that incident) rather than by GitHub's own protection.

## Pipeline map

| Workflow | Trigger(s) | Purpose | Gates what | Required status check? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ci.yml` | `push:main`, `pull_request`, `workflow_dispatch`, weekly cron (drift only) | lint/format/mypy/version/summary checks, test matrix (3 OS × 4 Python), packaging/MCP smoke, Docker build smoke, Windows CP1252 smoke, composite-action smoke, weekly unlocked drift canary | PR merge | Yes, for `code-quality`→"Code Quality & Static Analysis", `tests`→9 of 12 matrix cells (3.14 excluded), `packaging`, `windows-cp1252-pipe`, `action`. **Not** `container` or `drift`. |
| `provenance.yml` | `push:main`, `pull_request` | REUSE/SPDX license lint, zizmor workflow-security audit (SARIF to Code Scanning) | Nothing (not in required list) | No |
| `codeql.yml` | `push:main`, `pull_request`, `workflow_dispatch`, weekly cron | CodeQL `security-extended` over python/js-ts/actions | Nothing | No |
| `dependency-review.yml` | `pull_request` | Blocks newly-introduced vulnerable/incompatible deps in a diff | Nothing (not required) — real failures observed, see below | No |
| `dependency-audit.yml` | `pull_request:main`, weekly cron, `workflow_dispatch` | `pip-audit --strict` over the whole installed tree incl. extras; generates CycloneDX SBOM | Nothing, deliberately (comment: "turns the run red for a reviewer, not the merge button") | No |
| `dependabot-triage.yml` | `pull_request: [opened, reopened]` from dependabot only | Labels + manual-merge comment (auto-merge removed) | N/A | No |
| `lockfile.yml` | `pull_request` (paths: pyproject.toml/uv.lock), `workflow_dispatch` | `uv lock --check`, uploads/optionally commits a refreshed lock | Overlaps with `ci.yml`'s own `uv export --locked` | No, but overlaps `packaging`'s `uv lock --check` |
| `benchmark.yml` | `push:main,develop`, `pull_request`, `workflow_dispatch` | Runs `benchmark_runner.py --ci`, regression-gates task accuracy ≥80% | PR merge | Yes (both OS cells) |
| `perf.yml` | weekly cron, `workflow_dispatch` | `perf_bench.py --check` vs CPU-calibrated baseline | Nothing | No |
| `examples.yml` | `workflow_dispatch` only | Regenerates `examples/`, uploads artifact for human PR | N/A | No |
| `index-repo.yml` | `workflow_dispatch` | Index an arbitrary external repo via the composite action; optional release attach | N/A (admin tool) | No |
| `self-index.yml` | `push:main`, weekly cron, `workflow_dispatch` | Re-index this repo, push to `graph` branch | N/A | No |
| `prod-igy.yml` | `pull_request_target: [opened,synchronize,reopened]`, `issue_comment`, `workflow_dispatch` | AI/deterministic PR triage, labels, rebase/conflict nudges | N/A | No |
| `vscode.yml` | `push:main`/`pull_request` (paths: editors/vscode, repo2graph, self), `workflow_dispatch` | Compiles & tests the VS Code extension against the real MCP server (2 OS) | Nothing in the required list (extension has no CI gate on `main`) | No |
| `publish.yml` | `workflow_dispatch` only | **The entire release**: version bump → signed commit → release PR → re-verify checks → tag → PyPI → MCP Registry → GitHub Release → floating major tag → npm | The release itself | N/A (not a PR check) |

### Lifecycle diagram

```
 PR opened  ──► ci.yml (code-quality, tests×12, packaging, container,
                        windows-cp1252-pipe, action)
            ──► benchmark.yml (2 OS)
            ──► provenance.yml (reuse, zizmor)      \
            ──► codeql.yml                            > NOT required to merge
            ──► dependency-review.yml                /  (informational only)
            ──► dependency-audit.yml (if touches deps)
            ──► prod-igy.yml (triage/labels, pull_request_target)
            ──► lockfile.yml (if pyproject/uv.lock touched)
            ──► vscode.yml (if editors/vscode or repo2graph touched)
                 │
                 ▼  (required checks green per ruleset 22778968;
                      3.14 cells and `container` are NOT gating)
            merge to main (squash/merge/rebase; RepositoryRole-5 bypass always available,
                            enforce_admins=false)
                 │
                 ▼
            ci.yml / self-index.yml / vscode.yml / codeql.yml etc. re-run on main
                 │
     (human) workflow_dispatch → publish.yml
                 │
   prepare-release: bump_version.py auto → check_version.py + full pytest on
   bumped tree → commit via GraphQL (signed) → release PR → poll up to 60 min
   for CLEAN/merge → merge → RE-CHECK required checks before tagging → tag
                 │
        ┌────────┼─────────────┐
        ▼        ▼             ▼
      pypi     npm (after    mcp-registry (after pypi)
   (OIDC,      pypi)              │
   attest)        \               ▼
        \          \          release (GitHub Release + floating vN tag,
         \          \          needs pypi+mcp-registry)
          \          └──────────────┘
           ▼
      (no docker publish step anywhere)
      (no VS Code Marketplace / open-vsx publish step anywhere)
```

## Quality gate coverage

- **ruff check**: enforced, `ci.yml` `code-quality` job, `--output-format=github`
  (inline PR annotations). No `continue-on-error`.

## Release & publish pipeline analysis

`publish.yml` is `workflow_dispatch`-only by design, explicitly to avoid a
self-retriggering loop from its own `push:tags:` / `release:published` side
effects (documented in the file header, confirmed against the mcp-publisher
"cannot publish duplicate version" hard-failure case). The `branch` input
(default `main`) exists specifically because an earlier version of this
workflow bumped whatever branch was dispatched from but opened the PR against
a hardcoded `main`, letting the tag and the published artifact disagree about
content — now fixed by reading `inputs.branch` everywhere.

**Version derivation**: `bump_version.py auto` scans commits since the last
`vX.Y.Z` tag plus the `[Unreleased]` CHANGELOG section for `!:`/`BREAKING
CHANGE:`/`### Breaking`/`### Removed` (major), `feat:` (ignoring
`ci/test/docs/chore` scopes) or `### Added` (minor), else patch. **Malformed
commit header**: a header that doesn't match any of these patterns falls
through to the patch-bump default — safe but silently wrong if a contributor
actually meant a feature and used a non-conventional message; there's no hard
failure, only a possibly-too-small bump. **Missing CHANGELOG entry**: if there
are zero commits since the tag *and* an empty `[Unreleased]` section,
`detect_bump_type()` raises `RuntimeError` and the run fails before anything
is touched — correct fail-closed behaviour. If commits exist but
`[Unreleased]` is empty, `bump_changelog()` still synthesizes a minimal
`### Changed` section so the `release` job's CHANGELOG-section extractor
doesn't later fail on a tagged, merged commit — a deliberate design choice
to avoid repeating the exact 3.0.0 failure mode (see below) for a different
missing-input case.

**The exact 3.0.0 incident** is still documented in the workflow itself: the
bump used to be gated only *after* commit/tag; `tests/test_export_hardening.py`
asserted a static fallback version string that only the bump itself could
falsify, so the first run able to see the failure was the already-tagged
`pypi` job (`1 failed, 2073 passed`). `prepare-release` now runs
`check_version.py` and the full `pytest -q -n auto` against the bumped tree
*before* anything is committed, pushed, PR'd or tagged — a real fix, not just
a comment.

**Idempotency / resumability**:
- Tag creation is guarded (`git rev-parse -q --verify refs/tags/$tag`) — a
  re-run against an already-tagged commit won't double-tag.
- PR creation checks for an existing PR by head/base before creating.
- PyPI upload uses `skip-existing: true` specifically because the `release`
  job's `gh release create` re-fires this same workflow's `release:
  types:[published]`... wait, no — the workflow is explicitly
  `workflow_dispatch`-only and the header comment says this exact scenario
  ("every successful release re-triggered itself") was the *reason* the
  `push:tags:`/`release:published` triggers were removed. `skip-existing`
  now exists as defense-in-depth against a manual re-dispatch of an
  already-published tag, not because of a live self-trigger.
- `mcp-registry` hard-fails on a duplicate version (no skip-existing
  equivalent) — the one non-idempotent leg. A re-dispatch after a partial
  failure where PyPI succeeded but MCP registry did not would need the
  publish step itself to already be idempotent on GitHub's side; worth
  confirming `mcp-publisher publish` behaves the same way (not inspected here,
  recommend Agent verifying mcp-publisher's CLI docs).
- `npm` publish checks `npm view ...@$VERSION` first and exits 0 cleanly if
  already published; also exits 0 (with a warning, not a failure) if
  `NPM_TOKEN` is unset — meaning an npm publish can *silently no-op* and the
  overall workflow still reports green (see CI-05).
- The floating major tag (`vN`) is force-pushed every run (`git tag -f`,
  `push -f`), so that leg is naturally idempotent/resumable.

**Can PyPI/npm/MCP-Registry/GitHub-Release drift out of sync?** Yes, in two
concrete ways:
1. `npm`'s silent no-op on missing `NPM_TOKEN` (and `release`'s job dependency
   graph: `release` depends on `[prepare-release, pypi, mcp-registry]` but
   **not** on `npm`) means a release can complete successfully — tag pushed,
   GitHub Release created, PyPI and MCP Registry published — while npm quietly
   never got the new version, and nothing in the run fails to signal this.
2. There is no workflow anywhere that publishes a Docker image or a VS Code
   Marketplace release, so whatever process (if any) keeps those in sync with
   the PyPI/npm version is entirely outside this repository's CI and
   unverifiable from here.

**`commit_release_via_api.py`**: exists because `git commit` on an Actions
runner is never marked "Verified" even with an authenticated bot/App token,
and `main`'s current *classic* branch protection and the active ruleset both
require... (checked: the ruleset's `pull_request` rule does not list signed
commits as a requirement at the API level I could read, but the script's own
docstring states the release branch requires signed commits and that an
unsigned commit blocks every auto-merge attempt). It switched from the Git
Data API (blobs+trees+commits, never signed) to GraphQL
`createCommitOnBranch` (always signed) after discovering every release commit
produced before 2026-09-21 was unsigned and only ever merged via admin bypass
— this is the same incident the user's memory notes reference
(admin-bypass-merged-red-release-pr). The staging-branch dance
(`{branch}-signing-staging`) exists solely so an *existing* open PR's head
branch is never reset to empty mid-flight (which would auto-close the PR) —
a subtle, correct piece of engineering.

## Artifact integrity & provenance

- **`provenance.yml`** is misleadingly named for what it does: it runs REUSE
  license/SPDX linting and `zizmor` (workflow security static analysis,
  SARIF → Code Scanning). It does **not** produce SLSA provenance/attestation
  for any published artifact. The only real attestation in the pipeline is
  `pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish ... attestations: true` (PyPI Trusted
  Publishing OIDC attestation) and npm's `--provenance` flag (npm's own OIDC
  provenance, not SLSA). There is no `actions/attest-build-provenance` or
  equivalent SLSA generator anywhere in `.github/workflows/`.
- **SBOM**: `dependency-audit.yml` generates a CycloneDX SBOM via
  `pip-audit --format cyclonedx-json`, uploaded as a 14-day CI artifact. It is
  **not** attached to the GitHub Release, not published alongside the PyPI
  package, and only covers the Python dependency tree with `[dev,rag,mcp]`
  extras — it does not cover the npm launcher's dependency tree or the VS Code
  extension's.
- **Lockfile enforcement**: `uv.lock` currency is checked in three independent
  places — `ci.yml`'s `packaging` job (`uv lock --check`, hard fail),
  `lockfile.yml` (dedicated PR-triggered check with an auto-fix artifact and
  optional dispatch auto-commit), and implicitly by every `uv export --locked`
  call across `ci.yml`/`publish.yml`/`vscode.yml` (fails rather than
  re-resolving on drift). This is solid, if slightly redundant (CI-06).
- **Docker image**: built and smoke-tested in `ci.yml`'s `container` job only.
  Never pushed anywhere, and (CI-01) not even a required status check on
  `main`'s ruleset.

## Findings

**CI-01 — Severity: High. Confidence: High.**
Location: `main`'s active ruleset (`gh api .../rulesets/22778968`, rule type
`required_status_checks`) vs. `.github/workflows/ci.yml:135-144,294-299,363-368`.
Description: The ruleset's required contexts list `Test Suite (ubuntu-latest,
Python 3.11|3.12|3.13)`, `(macos-latest, ...)`, `(windows-latest, ...)` — nine
entries, exactly the 3.11–3.13 cross-product — but `ci.yml`'s matrix runs
twelve cells including Python 3.14. It also omits `Container Image Build &
Read-Only Smoke Test` entirely. `enforce_admins` is `false` and
`bypass_actors` grants `RepositoryRole 5` (effectively any repo admin)
`bypass_mode: "always"`.
Failure scenario: A PR that breaks the package on Python 3.14 (a version the
project ships classifiers for) or that breaks the Dockerfile can be merged to
`main` by a normal contributor with a fully green merge button, because
neither failing job is a required check. This is exactly the shape of the
3.0.0 admin-bypass incident, minus the admin: no bypass is even needed for
these two specific cells.
Recommendation: Add the four missing contexts (`Test Suite (ubuntu-latest,
Python 3.14)`, `(macos-latest, 3.14)`, `(windows-latest, 3.14)`, `Container
Image Build & Read-Only Smoke Test`) to the ruleset's `required_status_checks`
list. Separately, evaluate whether `enforce_admins`/ruleset bypass should stay
"always" given the documented admin-bypass-merged-red-release-pr incident.
Effort: Low (an API/UI change), but needs explicit maintainer sign-off since
it changes who can merge what.

**CI-02 — Severity: High. Confidence: Medium.**
Location: entire `.github/workflows/` tree; no Docker-registry push step
exists anywhere (confirmed via `grep -rn "docker push\|docker/login\|docker/build-push\|ghcr.io" .github/`
returning nothing) and no VS Code Marketplace/open-vsx publish step exists
(`grep -rn "vsce publish\|ovsx" .github/ editors/vscode/package.json` returning
nothing).
Description: Per the audit brief, this project "ships to PyPI, npm, Docker, a
GitHub Action and a VS Code extension." `publish.yml` publishes to PyPI, the
MCP Registry, and npm, and implicitly "publishes" the GitHub Action by tagging
(consumers pin `@vN`/`@vX.Y.Z`). It does not publish a Docker image to any
registry, and no workflow publishes the VS Code extension to any marketplace.
Failure scenario: Either (a) these two surfaces are not actually published
anywhere, and documentation/README claims about them are stale or aspirational
(worth cross-checking against Agent 1/Agent 6's findings on README claims), or
(b) they are published through a process entirely outside version control —
unauditable, unreproducible, and with no guaranteed correspondence to the
PyPI/npm version tagged in the same release. Either way, `CHANGELOG.md:788`
itself documents a prior, related incident: "Clarified Docker container build
expectations in SECURITY.md and README.md, removing stale claims of PR CI
building images" — i.e. this exact category of claim has drifted from reality
before.
Recommendation: Either wire a `docker/build-push-action` + registry login step
into `publish.yml` (gated the same way `npm`/`pypi` are, with the same
`needs: pypi` ordering) and a `vsce publish`/`ovsx publish` step for the
extension, or update every doc/README claim to explicitly state these are not
CI-published artifacts.
Effort: Medium (new credentials/secrets, registry choice, and
`version_surfaces.py` would need both as new surfaces).

**CI-03 — Severity: Medium. Confidence: High.**
Location: `.github/workflows/publish.yml:597-645` (`npm` job),
`publish.yml:486-489` (`release` job's `needs:`).
Description: The `npm` job exits 0 with only a `::warning::` when `NPM_TOKEN`
is unset, and the `release` job (which creates the GitHub Release and advances
the floating major tag) depends on `[prepare-release, pypi, mcp-registry]` —
not on `npm`. 
Failure scenario: If `NPM_TOKEN` is ever unset, rotated-and-not-updated, or
expired, the overall `publish.yml` run reports fully green, a GitHub Release
is cut, PyPI and the MCP Registry get the new version, and npm silently does
not — with no run-level failure, and only a step-level `::warning::` that
nobody is required to read. `npm/package.json`'s version (checked against the
release version in the step above it) would still match the *intended*
version even though the publish never happened, so the drift is invisible
until a user tries `npx repo2graph-mcp@latest` and gets the old version.
Recommendation: Make the missing-token case a hard failure (or at minimum
surface it in `release`'s job summary / via a required `needs: npm` with
`if: always()` reconciliation step) rather than a silent warning-and-continue.
Effort: Low.

**CI-04 — Severity: Medium. Confidence: Medium.**
Location: `.github/workflows/provenance.yml` (whole file, both jobs);
no `actions/attest-build-provenance` or SLSA generator anywhere in
`.github/workflows/`.
Description: `provenance.yml` is named for SLSA-style supply-chain provenance
but contains REUSE/license linting and zizmor workflow-security scanning —
useful, but not provenance. The only genuine attestation signal in the whole
pipeline is PyPI's own OIDC Trusted-Publishing attestation
(`gh-action-pypi-publish ... attestations: true`) and npm's `--provenance`
flag, both of which are provider-side features rather than something this
repo's CI explicitly generates and can verify.
Failure scenario: A consumer or security reviewer searching for "where does
this project produce SLSA provenance" finds a workflow named exactly that and
concludes (incorrectly) that build provenance is covered, when in fact no
in-repo step attests to *how* the wheel/sdist/npm package was built beyond
what PyPI/npm infer from the OIDC-authenticated job identity.
Recommendation: Either rename `provenance.yml` to reflect what it actually
does (`workflow-compliance.yml` or similar) to avoid the misleading signal, or
add an explicit `actions/attest-build-provenance` step in the `pypi`/`npm`
jobs and surface the attestation URL in the release summary.
Effort: Low (rename) to Medium (add real attestation).

**CI-05 — Severity: Low. Confidence: High.**
Location: `.github/workflows/lockfile.yml` (whole file) vs.
`.github/workflows/ci.yml:294-319` (`packaging` job's `lock_check` step).
Description: Both workflows independently run `uv lock --check` against the
same `pyproject.toml`/`uv.lock` pair on every PR that touches either file —
`lockfile.yml` is path-filtered to exactly `pyproject.toml`/`uv.lock`, so it
fires on precisely the PRs where `ci.yml`'s `packaging` job's own lock check
would already catch the same drift.
Failure scenario: Not a correctness bug — both will correctly fail together —
but it's redundant CI minutes and two separate red checks a contributor has to
reconcile for the same root cause, and `lockfile.yml` is not a required
status check so it adds signal noise without adding gate coverage `ci.yml`
doesn't already have.
Recommendation: Keep `lockfile.yml` only for its unique value (the
auto-generated-lockfile artifact upload and the dispatch auto-commit path);
consider dropping the pull_request trigger's duplicate check, or clearly scope
one of the two to be purely informational.
Effort: Low.

**CI-06 — Severity: Low. Confidence: Medium.**
Location: `.github/workflows/dependency-audit.yml:1-172` vs.
`.github/workflows/dependency-review.yml:1-23`.
Description: Both workflows gate on dependency vulnerabilities from two
different angles (installed-tree vs. diff-only) by design (documented in
`dependency-audit.yml`'s header), but neither is a required status check —
confirmed against the ruleset's `required_status_checks` list, which contains
neither "Dependency Supply Chain Review" nor the `dependency-audit.yml` job
name.
Failure scenario: A PR that introduces a newly-published high/critical CVE in
a new dependency can still merge with a fully green *required* check set,
because `dependency-review.yml`'s finding is informational only (matches the
file's own stated intent for `dependency-audit.yml`, but `dependency-review.yml`
carries no such caveat in its own comments — its omission from required
checks looks accidental rather than deliberate).
Recommendation: Confirm with maintainers whether `dependency-review.yml` (diff
of *newly introduced* deps, not the whole tree) was intentionally left out of
required checks; if not, add it — it is cheaper to require than
`dependency-audit.yml` since it only runs on the PR's own diff.
Effort: Low.

**CI-07 — Severity: Informational. Confidence: Medium (cross-reference to Agent 4).**
Location: `gh api repos/Srinivasan-78/repo2graph/rulesets/22778968` —
`bypass_actors: [{"actor_id":5,"actor_type":"RepositoryRole","bypass_mode":"always"}]`,
and classic branch protection (`gh api .../branches/main/protection`) shows
`enforce_admins.enabled: false` and a *separate*, much narrower
`required_status_checks.contexts: ["License & Copyright Compliance
(REUSE/SPDX)"]` (the classic API's stale view of the one check that used to
gate before the ruleset took over — note this is cross-referenced for context
only, not re-litigated here since branch-protection/bypass depth is Agent 4's
primary scope).
Description: The classic branch-protection API and the active ruleset
disagree about what's required — the classic endpoint still reports the
single pre-ruleset check as its `required_status_checks`, which is misleading
to anyone reading only that endpoint (e.g. third-party tooling, compliance
scanners) rather than the ruleset.
Recommendation: For CI/CD-reliability purposes specifically: any tooling or
documentation that asserts "these are the required checks" by querying the
classic protection endpoint instead of the ruleset will be wrong. Make sure
internal docs/scripts (if any exist) read rulesets, not classic protection.
Effort: Low.

## Contributor workflow verification

- `.github/CONTRIBUTING.md` exists (1155 lines) and `Makefile` defines
  `install` (`pip install -e ".[dev,rag,mcp]"`), `lint` (`ruff check .`),
  `format`/`format-check`, `typecheck` (`python -m mypy repo2graph/`, whole
  package — deliberately not a hand-maintained subset, per its own comment),
  `test` (`pytest -q -n auto`), `test-serial`, `test-cov`, and `clean`. Every
  target a contributor would need (`install`→`lint`→`format-check`→
  `typecheck`→`test`) exists and maps directly onto what `ci.yml`'s
  `code-quality` and `tests` jobs run — `ruff check .`, `ruff format --check
  .`, `mypy --platform <p> repo2graph` (CI iterates three platforms; `make
  typecheck` runs the host's own platform only — a predictable, documented gap
  noted in `ci.yml`'s own comment, not a bug), and `pytest -q -n auto
  --cov=repo2graph --cov-report=term-missing`. Running `make -n test` and
  `make -n typecheck` (not `make test` itself, per the read-only constraint)
  confirms the exact commands Make would issue match these.
- **CI vs. local install drift**: `ci.yml`'s `code-quality`/`tests` jobs install
  via `uv export --locked ... | pip install --require-hashes` (hashed, locked),
  while `Makefile install` and several lighter-weight workflows
  (`benchmark.yml`, `perf.yml`, `examples.yml`, the `drift` job in `ci.yml`,
  `index-repo.yml`) use plain `pip install -e ".[dev,rag,mcp]"` or similar —
  unlocked. This is a real, acknowledged, and *intentional* split: the locked
  path is what gates PRs, the unlocked path is specifically what `drift` exists
  to exercise (catch upstream breakage), and `Makefile`'s unlocked `install`
  is the fast local-dev path. Not a defect, but worth knowing that `make
  install && make test` does not reproduce byte-for-byte what the required
  `tests` job installs — a contributor chasing a CI-only failure should
  reproduce with `uv export --locked ...` + `pip install --require-hashes`,
  not plain `make install`.
- **Pre-commit vs. CI**: `.pre-commit-config.yaml` runs `ruff --fix
  --exit-non-zero-on-fix`, `ruff-format --check`, several file-hygiene hooks,
  a local `version-consistency` hook (`check_version.py`, triggered on the
  exact file set `version_surfaces.py` lists) and a local `mypy-strict` hook
  scoped to `^repo2graph/.*\.py$` using the same `pyproject.toml`
  `[[tool.mypy.overrides]]` CI uses. Passing `pre-commit run --all-files`
  locally is therefore a reasonably faithful predictor of the `code-quality`
  job (same tools, same scope, same config) — it does not run the test suite,
  the packaging smoke test, the Docker smoke test, or the multi-OS matrix, all
  of which are separate CI jobs by design, not gaps in pre-commit.

## Limitations

- Did not inspect `.github/scripts/summary.py` or `prod-igy.js` line-by-line
  (read their callers and the associated tests' existence/names only); a
  deeper logic review of those two scripts was out of time budget and they are
  lower-risk (summary rendering, PR triage) than the release pipeline.
- Did not independently verify `[tool.coverage.run] fail_under = 80` inside
  `pyproject.toml` — taken from `ci.yml`'s own comments; flagged for
  cross-check against Agent 2's code-quality report if not already covered.
- Could not verify whether a Docker image or VS Code extension is actually
  published through some out-of-repo process (a maintainer's local `docker
  push` / `vsce publish`, a separate private pipeline, a marketplace listing
  maintained by hand) — only that no workflow file in this repository does it.
  This should be confirmed directly with the maintainer rather than assumed
  either way.
- Did not run `pytest`, did not trigger/cancel/dispatch any workflow, did not
  modify branch protection, rulesets, or any repository setting — all `gh`
  calls used were read-only (`run list/view --log-failed`, `api ... ` GET
  only).
- Run-history statistics are drawn from the last 100 runs across *all*
  workflows in the repo as of 2026-11-01; this is a short window for
  workflows that run rarely (e.g. `publish.yml` — only 5 dispatches visible
  total) and may not capture older incidents referenced in project history
  (the 3.0.0 abort, the aborted-release tag-move) since those predate the
  current `prepare-release` gate-before-tag logic and are not reflected in
  current run conclusions.

Repository: Srinivasan-78/repo2graph. All `gh` calls were read-only (`list`/`view`/`api` GET). No GitHub state was modified. No repo files other than this one were written; no git state was changed; `pytest` was not run.

## Summary & repository issue statistics

- **Total issues (state=all, limit 600): 272.** All 272 are `CLOSED`. **Open issues: 0.**
- Issue numbers span 21 → 525, but the tracker is **not** 272 sequential issues — numbers are shared with PRs in one counter (GitHub issues+PRs share a repo-wide number sequence), so "numbered into the 500s" reflects 272 issues interleaved with 256 PRs (total 529 numbered items), not 525 issues.
- **Every issue (272/272) was authored by the repo owner, `Srinivasan-78`.** Zero issues were externally filed, despite the repo having public contributors on PRs. This is a maintainer-self-audit pattern, not a community bug tracker.
- Label taxonomy observed: `bug` (133), `enhancement` (122), `priority/P2` (110), `priority/P3` (85), `security` (74), `priority/P1` (52), `documentation` (41), `area/mcp` (27), `type/feat` (24), `backlog` (24), `area/graph` (23), `priority/high` (21 — legacy/alternate scheme predating `priority/P*`), `type/fix` (18), `type/ci` (16), `performance` (14), `good first issue` (13), `type/refactor` (12), `area/cli` (11), `area/workflows` (10), `question` (8), `area/docs` (6), `area/query` (6), `area/tests` (4), `type/chore` (4), `docs` (4), `type/docs` (3), `area/walker` (2), `help wanted` (2), plus singletons (`dependencies`, `chore`, `area/action`, `area/embed`).
- **No `priority/P0` issue exists in the history** — the project has apparently never classified anything as P0, or P0 issues (if any existed) were filed and resolved without that exact label, or the label itself was never used despite its presence in the taxonomy description given to this agent.
- **Pull requests (state=all, limit 600): 256 total.** 198 `MERGED`, 58 `CLOSED` (unmerged). No open PRs.
- PR author breakdown: `Srinivasan-78` 175, `app/dependabot` 30, `dyk1454683243-sudo` 30 (an automated fix-generation account, not a human contributor — see PR analysis), `app/prod-igy-bot` 11 (release-automation bot), and genuine external human contributors: `AbhishekKallolimath` (2), `llllgt` (1), `theluckystrike` (1), `Savage676` (1), `Parsiffall1` (1), `DYNOSuprovo` (1), `HarshRajSinghania` (1, closed/unmerged), `adnandispatch9-jpg` (1, closed/unmerged), `gane5hvarma` (1, closed/unmerged).
- Security advisories: **3**, all `closed` (GHSA-6wrx-c2rg-mvm9 medium — `verify_artifacts` path-traversal oracle; GHSA-f896-f643-87cf medium — OIDC `jwks_uri` not origin-constrained; GHSA-mqm8-mc66-wjvj high — OIDC JWKS fetch HTTP-redirect downgrade).
- Dependabot alerts: **37 total, all `fixed`, 0 open.** Severity split: 1 critical, 11 high, 18 medium, 7 low. (Consistent with the memory note that the alert-count toggle doesn't rescan — these are genuinely resolved, not hidden.)
- Discussions: **disabled/empty** — `gh api repos/Srinivasan-78/repo2graph/discussions` returned `[]`.
- Releases: 15 tags from `v1.2.0` (2026-09-09) to `v5.0.0` (2026-11-01, latest), consistent with the automated `publish.yml` release cadence noted in memory.

## Issue lifecycle analysis

Every issue in the tracker is closed, and every issue was filed by the owner — this is used as a self-audit log, not a public bug queue: the owner files a tightly-scoped `[P#] <symptom>` issue (often several in a single sitting, numbered consecutively — e.g. #500–#514, #523–#525), fixes it the same day or within a few days, and closes with a one-line comment naming the resolving commit hash. There is no triage lag, no stale-issue backlog, and no issue left unaddressed — on paper. The catch (see Regressions section) is that "closed with a commit hash" is **not independently re-verified against the working tree** by this process; it is trusted at face value.

Clustering: issues are frequently batch-filed and batch-fixed in groups of 2–5 against a single commit (`fcfece04` resolved both #513 and #514; `516fe12d` resolved #523, #524, and #525 together). This is efficient but creates exactly the risk realized in the regression below: a single revert of that commit's working tree re-breaks multiple issues at once, and nothing detects that the issues are still marked closed.

## Pull request analysis

- 198/256 PRs merged, 58 closed unmerged, 0 open.
- Of the 58 closed-unmerged PRs, 30 are from `app/dependabot` (routine dependency bumps superseded by newer bump PRs — expected churn, not abandoned work) and most of the remainder are from the automated account `dyk1454683243-sudo`, which filed ~30 narrowly-scoped `fix(<area>): ...` PRs (e.g. #170–#231) that were individually closed unmerged.
- **This is not evidence of abandoned fixes.** Spot-checked: PRs #413–#416 ("secrets lowercase detection", "namespace separators", "ci hardening", "docs") were all closed unmerged, but `git log` shows commit `67e15bbf` — *"Combine #413, #414, #415 and #416: parser and secret-scanner fixes, workflow hardening, packaging and security docs (#418)"* — which **is** merged (PR #418, merged 2026-09-25). The repo's workflow (consistent with the "Solo-account merge gates" memory note) is: open several small bot/automation PRs, close them individually, and land the combined diff through a single PR that passes the required-signature/merge gates. Similarly, PR #476 ("Security hardening, audit fixes, and retrieval/MCP improvements") was closed unmerged but its named features (`[tool.repo2graph]` config file, `TESTS`/`USES_FIXTURE` edges, MCP pagination cursors) are all verified present in the current tree (`repo2graph/config.py`, `tests/test_tests_edges.py`, `tests/test_mcp_pagination.py`) — so it too landed via other, smaller merged PRs rather than being abandoned.
- Genuine human external contributions are small (docs, one language-support PR, one test-coverage PR, one map-checksum fix) and all either merged or trivially closed (duplicate/typo PRs like #91 vs #93 "recognize .mts/.cts as TypeScript", both closed, functionality present under #92's sibling work — not independently reconfirmed here, flagged as low-confidence).
- No closed-unmerged PR surveyed carries content this agent could positively identify as **lost** (i.e., a real fix that never landed anywhere). Given the volume (58 PRs), this is a sampled conclusion, not exhaustive — see Limitations.

## Discussions, advisories, Dependabot alerts, releases

- **Discussions:** disabled or never used — API returns an empty array, no error. Cannot be used as a signal source.
- **Security advisories (3, all closed):**
  - GHSA-6wrx-c2rg-mvm9 (medium) — `verify_artifacts()` treated manifest.json checksum keys as trusted paths → arbitrary file read / hash-disclosure oracle via `repo2graph doctor`. Reachable via `doctor.py:414`.
  - GHSA-f896-f643-87cf (medium) — OIDC `jwks_uri` not constrained to the issuer's origin.
  - GHSA-mqm8-mc66-wjvj (high) — OIDC JWKS fetch could be downgraded to cleartext via HTTP redirect, enabling token forgery.
  - All three are in the auth/OIDC and integrity-verification subsystems — consistent with `auth`/`jwt`/`jwks` being a recurring theme in the issue titles (19 and 5 keyword hits respectively, see index below).
- **Dependabot alerts:** 37 total, all state `fixed`, 0 currently open. No permission error encountered (the token has `security_events`/alerts read access in this session).
- **Releases:** 15 releases, v1.2.0 → v5.0.0, latest v5.0.0 tagged 2026-11-01T11:45:43Z — i.e., **the v5.0.0 release was cut the same day this audit is running**, which is worth flagging to the orchestrator: whatever the uncommitted working-tree regression described below is, it has NOT yet been released (it's uncommitted), but the repository is mid-release-cycle.

## Per-issue investigation

Format: Issue #, Title, State, Classification, Fix commit, Verification method and result, Confidence.

### #523 — "[P2] Class-level pytest fixtures are dropped during framework graph construction"
- **State:** CLOSED. **Classification: REGRESSION** (previously verified fixed; now reproducible again if the working tree is committed as-is).
- **Fix commit:** `516fe12d` ("fix: resolve #523 (class fixture scoping), #524 ..., #525 ...").
- **Original problem:** `extract_pytest_facts()` in `repo2graph/frameworks.py` didn't record the enclosing class on fixture records, so `_find_symbol(f["fn_name"], None, ...)` in `graph.py` couldn't match class-scoped fixture symbols (whose actual parent was the class), causing the fixture to be dropped entirely (no `is_fixture=True`, no `USES_FIXTURE` edges, breaking `--affected-tests` for class-scoped suites). The fix additionally required class fixtures to be visible only within their class and to shadow outer fixtures.
- **Verification method and result:** Read `git diff -- repo2graph/frameworks.py`. The committed fix at `516fe12d` built a `cls_qualname = f"{enclosing_class}.{cls_name}" if enclosing_class else cls_name"` and used that qualname for nested-class fixture registration/walk. **The current uncommitted working tree reverts this**: it drops the qualname construction and uses the bare `cls_name` again, exactly the pre-fix state. This is a verbatim revert of the fix for nested/qualified class scoping.
- **Confidence:** High (direct diff read against the issue's described root cause).

### #524 — "[P2] SqliteGraphStore fails in multi-threaded environments (MCP/ThreadPool) with sqlite3.ProgrammingError and leaks handles on Windows"
- **State:** CLOSED. **Classification: REGRESSION (partial).**
- **Fix commit:** `516fe12d`.
- **Original problem:** `sqlite3.connect(...)` lacked `check_same_thread=False`; no `__enter__`/`__exit__` on `SqliteGraphStore`/the `GraphStore` Protocol; `MemoryGraphStore` lacked `close()`/context-manager duck-typing; unclosed handles caused `PermissionError [WinError 32]` on Windows.
- **Verification method and result:** `git diff -- repo2graph/store.py`. The `check_same_thread=False` connect argument **is still present** (not reverted) — so the headline `sqlite3.ProgrammingError` symptom from the issue body would not reproduce. - **Confidence:** High. The regression is partial: the specific `sqlite3.ProgrammingError` cited in the issue text would not resurface (connect flag intact), but the lock removal and Protocol-method removal are direct reverts of the rest of the same commit, and the test was weakened to mask it.

The exact-match normalization fix for conftest path matching described in #525 is intact in the current working tree.
- **Confidence:** High (confirmed by absence of diff on the relevant file).

### #513 — "[P2] --affected-tests cannot see tests that consume a fixture by injection"
- **State:** CLOSED. **Classification: Previously reported and verified fixed — NOT regressed, but DEPENDENT on #523/#524's fixture-edge machinery.**
- **Fix commit:** `fcfece04` (separate from `516fe12d`; this issue predates and is foundational to #523's fix — #513 added the base `USES_FIXTURE` edge machinery and fixture parsing that #523 then had to extend for class scoping).

The base fixture-injection edge mechanism is present. However, because #523's class-scoping layer on top of this machinery is now reverted, **class-scoped fixture consumption specifically** (the scenario #523 was filed to cover) is broken again even though module/conftest-level fixture consumption (#513's original scenario) is not.
- **Confidence:** High for #513 itself being intact; the interaction with #523's regression is the important nuance for the orchestrator.

### Regression test confirmation
`tests/test_framework_edges.py::test_pytest_nested_classes_and_shadowed_fixtures` (lines 569–611) builds a repo with `conftest.py` defining `value`, and `tests/test_nested.py` with `class TestOuter: class TestInner:` containing a fixture `value(self, value)` that *overrides* the outer conftest fixture (classic fixture-shadowing pattern), plus `test_inner(self, value)` consuming the class-scoped override. The test asserts a `USES_FIXTURE` edge from `sym:...::TestOuter.TestInner.value` → `sym:conftest.py::value` (the override depending on the shadowed outer fixture) and from `...::TestOuter.TestInner.test_inner` → `...::TestOuter.TestInner.value` (the test using the class fixture). # Agent 2 — Code Quality & Maintainability Audit

Scope: `repo2graph` package (~32k LOC across `repo2graph/*.py` and `repo2graph/mcp/*.py`).
Security and correctness-bug analysis are explicitly out of scope (owned by other agents);
any suspected correctness bug noticed in passing is flagged briefly for Agent 3 and not
analysed further.

## Summary

Overall verdict: **this is an unusually disciplined codebase for its size** — lint and
strict-mypy are both fully clean, naming/comment conventions are consistent, magic numbers
are named constants, resource handling (files, sqlite connections, locks) is deliberately
guarded, and the long prose comments are (on every sample checked) accurate explanations of
non-obvious decisions rather than stale filler. The principal maintainability risk is **function
size and cyclomatic complexity concentrated in a handful of "god functions"** in the hottest
modules (`graph.py:build`, `query.py:pack_context`, `parse.py:parse_source`,
`graphdiff.py:find_affected_tests`), plus one module (`viz.py`) that is two-thirds an inline
HTML/JS string with no tooling coverage. These are real, measurable maintainability costs even
though the code inside them is individually careful.

### Metrics

- Package size: ~31,900 lines across 60 source files (`repo2graph/*.py` + `repo2graph/mcp/*.py`).
- Largest modules: `parse.py` 2300, `graph.py` 2172, `query.py` 2123, `cli.py` 2110,
  `export.py` 1698, `viz.py` 1328, `security.py` 1181, `mcp/server.py` 932, `answer.py` 880,
  `scip.py` 850, `graphdiff.py` 766, `integrity.py` 757, `discovery.py` 727.
- `ruff check .` (select `E,F,W,BLE,B,S,I,UP,RUF`, no `--fix`): **0 findings**.
- `python -m mypy repo2graph/` (strict, applies to all 59 own-package modules, no
  per-module overrides except `numpy`/`numpy.*` which only relaxes stub-following, not
  type checking of this package's code): **0 errors, 60 source files**.
- No `TODO`/`FIXME`/`XXX` markers anywhere in the package.
- `except Exception`/bare-except sites: 28, all narrowed with either a `# noqa: BLE001 -
  <rationale>` comment or an inline comment explaining the resilience boundary and the
  re-raise/fallback path taken. No swallow-to-silent-empty-result pattern found (see CQ-06
  for the one caveat).
- `type: ignore` comments: 8 in the whole package, each with the specific error code and a
  one-line reason.

## Findings

### CQ-01: `graph.build()` is a 792-line function with ~155 branch points

- **Severity**: High
- **Confidence**: High
- **Location**: `repo2graph/graph.py:1380`–`2172` (function `build`, runs to end of file)
- **Description**: `build()` is the single entry point that turns a parsed repo into a
  `Graph`. It is 792 lines long and contains roughly 155 `if`/`for`/`while`/`except`/`with`
  branch points (counted via AST walk), plus six nested closures defined inline
  (`scope_of` @1731, `named_in` @1757, `match_bases` @1763, `base_methods` @1785,
  `names_home` @1809, `tier3_imported` @1825) that implement successive call-resolution
  tiers (same-file, same-class-hierarchy, imported, same-module, …). Each closure captures
  a large amount of enclosing state (`by_name`, `by_name_path`, `members`, `imported_files`,
  `import_aliases`, `class_bases`, …), so none of them can be tested, reasoned about, or
  reused independently of the rest of `build()`.
- **Why it matters**: This is the core graph-construction logic for the whole tool. A
  function this size cannot be unit-tested at a granularity finer than "run the whole
  build," which is exactly the situation the existing comments describe fixing bugs around
  (e.g. the `#456 P2` quadratic-blowup comment at `graph.py:1744`). Every future change to
  name resolution has to be made inside this one function, with full knowledge of all of its
  state, raising the risk of an unintended interaction between tiers.
- **Recommendation**: Extract the six resolution-tier closures (and the sections that feed
  them: `by_name`/`by_name_path`/`by_name_dir`/`members` construction) into a small
  `_NameResolver` class or module-level functions taking their dependencies as explicit
  parameters instead of captured closure state. This does not need to change behavior — it
  is a pure decomposition — but it would let each tier be unit-tested and documented on its
  own.
- **Effort**: L

### CQ-02: `query.pack_context()` is 384 lines / ~89 branches; `retrieve()` is 116 lines

- **Severity**: Medium-High
- **Confidence**: High
- **Location**: `repo2graph/query.py:1537`–`1923` (`pack_context`), `1397`–`1517` (`retrieve`)
- **Description**: `pack_context` (the function that turns ranked chunks into the final
  cited context pack returned to an agent) is 384 lines with ~89 branch points, handling
  token-vs-character budgeting, map prepending, expansion, citation formatting, and
  truncation all in one body. `retrieve` (116 lines) is comparatively mild but still mixes
  BM25/vector fusion, reranking, lexical-weakness fallback, and test-seed demotion inline.
- **Why it matters**: `query.py` is on the critical path for every answer the tool
  produces; a bug here produces a wrong or truncated context pack silently (the kind of
  retrieval-correctness risk this audit was asked to flag). The function's size makes it
  hard to verify that every exit path still respects both the character and token budgets.
- **Recommendation**: Split `pack_context` along its already-visible phase boundaries
  (budget resolution → map prepend → per-chunk excerpting/citation → final fit) into
  private helpers with clear pre/postconditions, similar to the existing `_fit_lines`,
  `_compress`, `_excerpt_record`, `_cite_block` helpers already factored out below it —
  the pattern is already present, just not applied all the way through the main function.
- **Effort**: M

### CQ-03: Several other functions in hot-path modules exceed ~250 lines / ~45 branches

- **Severity**: Medium
- **Confidence**: High
- **Location** (lines = body length, branches = AST-counted `if/for/while/except/with` + bool-op joins):
  - `repo2graph/parse.py:1926` `parse_source` — 347 lines, ~104 branches
  - `repo2graph/graphdiff.py:343` `find_affected_tests` — 346 lines, ~83 branches
  - `repo2graph/chunks.py:201` `iter_chunks` — 293 lines, ~47 branches
  - `repo2graph/discovery.py:449` `explain_path` — 278 lines, ~28 branches
  - `repo2graph/parse.py:1654` `parse_import_details` — 256 lines, ~46 branches
  - `repo2graph/graph.py:1189` `add_pytest_fixture_edges` — 187 lines, ~51 branches
  - `repo2graph/graph.py:534` `_chunk_and_parse` — 178 lines, ~17 branches
  - `repo2graph/integrity.py:527` `verify_artifacts` — 173 lines, ~42 branches
  - `repo2graph/export.py:944` `write_manifest` — 176 lines
  - `repo2graph/mcp/server.py:766` `main` — 162 lines
- **Description**: These are long, multi-purpose functions in the modules this audit was
  asked to focus on (parse, graph, query, export, mcp/server, graphdiff, integrity,
  discovery, chunks). None individually is as extreme as CQ-01/CQ-02, but collectively they
  show the same pattern: a function handles discovery/validation/aggregation/formatting in
  one body instead of composed smaller units.
- **Why it matters**: Same class of risk as CQ-01/CQ-02 at smaller scale — harder to review
  a diff against, harder to unit test one concern in isolation, higher chance a change to
  one branch has an unintended effect on a sibling branch 200 lines away.
- **Recommendation**: No urgent action needed; treat as backlog cleanup opportunistically
  when next touching each function. `find_affected_tests` and `parse_source` would benefit
  most given their branch density.
- **Effort**: M (per function, if tackled)

### CQ-04: `viz.py` is two-thirds an inline HTML/CSS/JS string with no tooling coverage

- **Severity**: Medium
- **Confidence**: High
- **Location**: `repo2graph/viz.py:459`–`1328` (`TEMPLATE = r"""..."""`, to end of file; the
  module is 1328 lines total, so the template is ~870 of them, i.e. ~65%)
- **Description**: The interactive HTML visualization is authored as one large raw Python
  string literal containing a full HTML document with embedded `<style>` and `<script>`
  (JS) blocks. The `<script>` content is not run through any JS linter/formatter and is
  invisible to `ruff`/`mypy` entirely — it is just a string as far as Python tooling is
  concerned.
- **Why it matters**: Most of the module's substance (DOM logic, rendering, interaction
  handling for the viz output) has zero static analysis, no syntax highlighting in most
  editors' Python-mode, and cannot be tested except by rendering the page and exercising it
  manually/E2E. A typo in the JS fails silently in the browser console, not at build or
  lint time.
- **Recommendation**: Not urgent to change given it's a self-contained, rarely-touched
  template, but if the JS grows further, consider extracting it to a sibling `.js`/`.html`
  asset file embedded via `importlib.resources` at build time, which would let a JS
  linter (or at least basic syntax checking) run over it in CI.
- **Effort**: M

### CQ-05: `cli.py:main()` is 959 lines, almost entirely argparse wiring

- **Severity**: Low
- **Confidence**: High
- **Location**: `repo2graph/cli.py:1119`–`2078` (`main`)
- **Description**: `main()` is by line count the largest function in the package, but
  AST analysis shows ~182 `add_argument`/`add_parser` calls against only ~10 real branch
  points — it is overwhelmingly declarative parser construction, not complex control flow.
  Dispatch (`args.func(args)`) and top-level exception handling (`KeyboardInterrupt`,
  `BrokenPipeError`, `_GraphLimitExceeded`) sit at the very end.
- **Why it matters**: Despite low complexity, the sheer length makes `main()` slow to
  navigate (finding "where is the `--jobs` flag defined" means scrolling ~900 lines), and
  it is the one function in the file that cannot be tested without invoking the full CLI
  parser, since the parser-building and the dispatch logic are not separated.
  This is primarily a size/navigability issue, not a complexity one — tagging it `CQ`
  (not a style-only note) because it affects how easy the CLI surface is to extend safely.
- **Recommendation**: Factor parser construction (the `add_argument`/`add_parser` calls)
  into a `_build_parser() -> argparse.ArgumentParser` helper, leaving `main()` itself as
  just: build parser → parse args → dispatch → handle top-level exceptions. Purely
  mechanical, low risk.
- **Effort**: S

### CQ-06: Lint config has no complexity/length gate, so CQ-01..CQ-03 can grow unchecked

- **Severity**: Low
- **Confidence**: High
- **Location**: `pyproject.toml:184`–`205` (`[tool.ruff.lint]` `select = ["E", "F", "W",
  "BLE", "B", "S", "I", "UP", "RUF"]`)
- **Description**: The ruff rule selection is deliberate and well-justified by the adjacent
  comment (bug classes, security, import order, syntax upgrades), but it does not include
  McCabe complexity (`C90`) or pylint's `too-many-*`/`PLR09xx` rules. Nothing in CI would
  flag a function growing from 792 to 1,200 lines.
- **Why it matters**: Given CQ-01 through CQ-03 already exist, there is no automated
  backstop preventing further growth of the largest functions, which is how `build()`
  likely got to 792 lines in the first place (incremental additions, each individually
  reasonable).
- **Recommendation**: Consider adding `C90` with a generous `max-complexity` threshold
  (e.g. 25–30, deliberately above today's average so it only fires on genuine outliers) as
  a tripwire for future growth, without requiring an immediate refactor of the existing
  offenders. This is a process recommendation, not a correctness issue — purely optional.
- **Effort**: S

## Style observations (non-defects)

- The codebase makes heavy, consistent use of long prose docstrings/comments explaining
  *why* a decision was made (architecture rationale, historical bug numbers like `#456`,
  `#398`, `#341`). Every sample checked during this audit (`chunks.py:iter_chunks`'s claim
  about source-cache eviction, `frameworks.py`'s module docstring, `cache.py`'s TTL
  rationale, `fetch.py`'s memoization caveat) was verified against the actual code and
  found accurate, not stale. This is unusual for a codebase this size and is a genuine
  strength, not a smell — flagged here only because the audit brief asked to judge rather
  than assume.
- Private module-level `global` mutable state (`fetch.py:_git_version_cache`,
  `parse.py:_cpp_available_cache`, `parsepool.py:_slot/_watch/_worker_job`) is present but
  in every case is a deliberate, documented memoization or per-worker-process state pattern
  required by the multiprocessing design, with explicit comments about why a failed probe
  is *not* cached. Not flagged as a defect.
- Magic numbers in `query.py` (`BM25_B`, `BM25_AVG_LEN`, `CONTAINER_SEED_PENALTY`,
  `STEM_VARIANT_WEIGHT`, `TEST_SEED_PENALTY`) are already named module-level constants, not
  inline literals — good practice already followed.
- `main` is defined in both `cli.py` and `mcp/server.py`, `build` in both `graph.py` and
  `store.py`, `retrieve`/`pack_context` in both `federated.py` and `query.py` — checked all
  of these; none are duplicated logic. `federated.py`'s versions are thin fan-out wrappers
  that call into `Index.retrieve`/`Index.pack_context` per-repo and merge results; the
  `main` pair are each a module's own CLI/server entry point. No action needed.
- No `eval`/`exec`/`pickle` misuse found; the one `ast.literal_eval` use (`embed.py:126`)
  is on a trusted, self-written header format, not untrusted input.

## Tooling output

```
$ ruff check . --no-fix
All checks passed!
```

```
$ python -m mypy repo2graph/
Success: no issues found in 60 source files
```

## Strengths

- Zero ruff findings and zero mypy findings under `strict = true` with no per-module
  escape hatches for the package's own code (only `numpy`/`numpy.*` stub-following is
  relaxed) — the pyproject.toml comment at `pyproject.toml:273`–`284` documents that this is
  a deliberate, hard-won state (the last three modules, `cli.py`/`graph.py`/`parse.py`, were
  only recently brought under strict mode, and doing so surfaced two real bugs elsewhere).
- Resource handling (file opens, sqlite connections, lock files, subprocess pipes) is
  consistently guarded with context managers, explicit `__enter__`/`__exit__`, or
  errno-aware fallback paths (`graph.py:_safe_open`, `lock.py`'s `acquire()`,
  `store.py:SqliteGraphStore`).
- Exception handling, while broad `except Exception` appears 28 times, is in every
  instance deliberately scoped to a described "resilience boundary" with a comment
  explaining what failure mode is being contained and why it must not crash the caller;
  none degrade to a silently-wrong result without logging/propagating a reason.
- No dead code, no unused imports/variables, no `TODO`/`FIXME` backlog markers anywhere —
  the codebase appears to be kept clean continuously rather than audited occasionally.

## Limitations

- This audit sampled function-level complexity via line counts and an AST branch-counter
  (not a calibrated cyclomatic-complexity tool), so branch counts are approximate relative
  orderings, not exact McCabe numbers.
- Given the size of the package, "sample the rest" modules (tasks.py, cache.py, events.py,
  lock.py, bugreport.py, doctor.py, status.py, embed.py, imports.py, refcapture.py,
  cochange.py, exclusions.py, schema.py, explain.py, edgemeta.py, changelog.py, config.py,
  testpaths.py, tokenizers.py, rerank.py, watch.py, cli_embed.py, cli_inspect.py,
  neo4j.py, federated.py, audit.py, limits.py, and the remaining mcp/* modules) received a
  lighter pass (grep-based pattern search, not line-by-line reading) and could hide
  function-size or duplication issues not surfaced by the broad searches run here.
- Per the task's constraints, the four files with uncommitted changes
  (`frameworks.py`, `graph.py`, `store.py`, `tests/test_store.py`) were read in their
  current (modified) on-disk state but not diffed against HEAD for quality commentary,
  since those changes are explicitly another agent's/the user's in-flight work and were
  left untouched.

You are Agent 4 (Security & Vulnerability Assessment) in a multi-agent audit of E:\Github\repo2graph — a Python code-graph indexer + MCP server that reads arbitrary user source trees, can clone/fetch remote repos, scans for secrets, renders HTML visualisations, and exposes an MCP tool surface to LLM agents. This is a DEFENSIVE security review of the maintainer's own public repository.

ABSOLUTE RULES:
- READ-ONLY on every pre-existing file. No edits/writes/formatting of any existing file. Never `ruff format` / `--fix`. No git state changes.
- UNCOMMITTED changes exist in repo2graph/frameworks.py, graph.py, store.py, tests/test_store.py — leave untouched.
- Do NOT run the pytest suite. No destructive commands. No exploitation against any third party, no external network testing. Local static analysis and local-only reproductions in the scratchpad C:\Users\Srini\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\E--Github-repo2graph\41b9c827-517a-4445-9b19-c45c383d5b12\scratchpad only.
- REDACT any real secret you discover: report `path:line` + the kind of secret, never the value. If you find a live credential, flag it as CRITICAL with redacted evidence.
- The ONLY repo file you may write is: E:\Github\repo2graph\audit-reports\AGENT-FINDINGS\04-security.md

SCOPE — trust boundaries first. Enumerate them explicitly: untrusted source trees being indexed; untrusted repo URLs/refs (`repo2graph/fetch.py`); MCP tool arguments supplied by an LLM (`repo2graph/mcp/*`); config files in the target repo (`repo2graph/config.py`); CI workflow inputs; the generated HTML viz consumed in a browser; Neo4j/export sinks.

Review in depth:
- `repo2graph/security.py` (1181 lines — the secret scanner) and `tests/test_secrets_hardening.py`, `test_secret_coverage_gaps.py`: correctness of redaction, whether secrets can leak into the index, into query output, into exports, into the HTML viz, or into logs/error messages. A secret scanner that misses or that re-emits findings verbatim is a real finding.
- `repo2graph/mcp/guardrails.py`, `mcp/server.py`, `mcp/tools.py`, `mcp/schemas.py`, `mcp/resources.py`: argument validation, path confinement (can an MCP caller read files outside the indexed repo? directory traversal via node ids, chunk ids, file params, resource URIs?), resource exhaustion / unbounded responses, prompt-injection surface (indexed source content flowing into tool output that an agent will treat as instructions — assess whether output is delimited/neutralised; see tests/test_prompt_isolation.py).
- Path traversal and unsafe file ops repo-wide: `exclusions.py`, `discovery.py`, `export.py`, `fetch.py`, symlink following, `..` handling, absolute-path escapes, Windows device names/ADS, archive/zip handling if any.
- Command execution: every `subprocess`/`os.system`/`shell=True` call site (grep the whole repo incl. scripts/ and .github/scripts/) — argument injection via branch names, refs, paths, URLs. `fetch.py` git invocations are a prime target.
- Deserialisation: `pickle`, `yaml.load`, `eval`, `exec`, `marshal`, untrusted JSON into code paths. tree-sitter grammar loading.
- `repo2graph/viz.py` (1328 lines): HTML/JS generation from repo content — XSS via file names, symbol names, code snippets injected into the page or into JSON embedded in a script tag. Check escaping. See tests/test_viz_safety.py.
- Secret/credential handling: tokens for `github`/fetch, env var handling, tokens in error messages or saved artifacts, temp-file permissions (`tempfile` usage, predictable names), `.r2g` index file permissions.
- Cryptography/hashing use: is any hash used for security (vs. caching)? md5/sha1 in a security context.
- Insecure defaults; the "no network calls" promise in README/.github/SECURITY.md vs. reality (verify by grepping for network calls: urllib, requests, httpx, socket) — a violated security claim is a finding.
- GitHub Actions security: all files in `.github/workflows/` — `pull_request_target`, `permissions:` blocks (missing or over-broad), unpinned third-party actions (tag vs SHA), script injection via `${{ github.event.* }}` into `run:`, untrusted PR code execution, secret exposure to forks, artifact/cache poisoning, release artifact integrity & provenance (`provenance.yml`, `publish.yml`). Note `.github/zizmor.yml` exists — check whether findings are suppressed. If `zizmor` is installed you may run it read-only; if not, do the review manually and say so.
- Supply chain: note observations but Agent 10 owns dependencies in depth — don't duplicate, cross-reference.

Use OWASP framing where it fits. Run read-only greps/static checks; if `bandit`/`pip-audit`/`zizmor` are already installed you may run them (do NOT install anything new) and record exact output; if absent, state that explicitly as a limitation.

For EVERY finding: ID `SEC-01`…, Severity (CRITICAL/HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW/INFO), Confidence (Confirmed/High/Medium/Low), CWE where applicable, Location `path:line`, Attack scenario (who the attacker is, what they control, what they gain — be concrete about preconditions), Evidence (redacted as needed), Recommended remediation, Effort. Explicitly distinguish exploitable vulnerabilities from hardening gaps and defence-in-depth suggestions.
