input.content: # OBS Streaming Environment — Security & Reliability Review Review date: 2026-10-31 Scope: C:\Users\Srini\obs-tools, C:\Users\Srini\obs-overlays, C:\Users\Srini\AppData\Roaming\obs-studio, C:\Program Files\obs-studio\obs-plugins\64bit, C:\Users\Srini\obs-backups Mode: read-only. No files were modified, moved, or deleted during this review. All secret values below are REDACTED. Locations are given as file path + line number so the value can be found and rotated. --- ## Ranked Findings ### CRITICAL **C1. obs-websocket password stored in plaintext in at least 5 locations, and the service it unlocks is bound to ALL network interfaces, not loopback-only.** - `C:\Users\Srini\obs-tools\autopilot.config.json:4` — `"password": ""` - `C:\Users\Srini\obs-tools\backup-pre-agentselect-012817\autopilot.config.json:4` — same value, stray self-made backup *inside* obs-tools (not the official backup location, easy to forget about) - `C:\Users\Srini\AppData\Roaming\obs-studio\plugin_config\obs-websocket\config.json:5` — `"server_password": ""` (this is obs-websocket's own on-disk store; expected plugin behavior, but it's one more plaintext copy that any backup/sync tool will pick up) - `C:\Users\Srini\obs-backups\20261031-160039-baseline-pre-overhaul\obs-tools\autopilot.config.json:4` and `...\plugin_config\obs-websocket\config.json:5` — duplicated again by the baseline backup; every future `backup-obs.ps1` run will keep duplicating it Network exposure, confirmed directly from the OBS log (`AppData\Roaming\obs-studio\logs\2026-10-31 01-34-10.txt`): ``` 01:34:13.832: [obs-websocket] [WebSocketServer::Start] Not locked to IPv4 bindings 01:34:13.835: [obs-websocket] [WebSocketServer::Start] Server started successfully on port 4456. Possible connect address: 192.168.0.4 ``` This is the server's own startup banner: it is listening on **all interfaces** (0.0.0.0 / ::), not `127.0.0.1`, despite `autopilot.config.json`'s `"host": "127.0.0.1"` — that field only controls which address *autopilot's client* dials, it has no effect on where the obs-websocket *server* binds. obs-websocket's config.json / UI has no host-bind option at all; "all interfaces" is the plugin's only mode. `auth_required: true` is set, so a blind LAN attacker is stopped at the handshake — but the password that gates that handshake is sitting in plaintext in five files, three of which (`obs-tools`, the stray backup, and the baseline backup) are plain files with no OS-level encryption and get copied by `backup-obs.ps1` without redaction. Anyone who can read any one of those files, plus anyone on the same LAN/Wi-Fi segment at 192.168.0.4:4456, can authenticate and have full remote control of OBS (switch scenes, stop the stream, read the configured stream key once one is set, start a virtual camera, etc.). **Impact:** Full remote control of the streaming rig from anywhere on the local network, given either (a) local file read access, or (b) network+password access. Currently no stream key is configured so the most damaging leak (the Twitch stream key) isn't live yet, but the control-plane compromise is real today. **Remediation:** 1. Rotate the obs-websocket password (Tools → WebSocket Server Settings → Generate Password) once the plaintext copies are being cleaned up. 2. Move the password out of `autopilot.config.json` into a value that isn't committed/backed-up in the clear — e.g. Windows Credential Manager (`keyring` Python package) or an environment variable set outside the repo tree, read at process start. 3. Delete `C:\Users\Srini\obs-tools\backup-pre-agentselect-012817\` once it's no longer needed — it's a second, forgotten plaintext copy outside of the sanctioned backup directory. 4. If LAN exposure is not needed (it almost certainly isn't — autopilot, obs-meter.js, and all browser sources only ever dial 127.0.0.1), add a Windows Firewall **inbound block rule** for TCP 4456 from non-loopback sources, since obs-websocket itself cannot be told to bind to loopback only. 5. Going forward, `backup-obs.ps1` should either exclude `plugin_config/obs-websocket/config.json` and `obs-tools/autopilot.config.json`, or the backup directory should be treated as equally sensitive as the live config (ACL'd, not synced to cloud storage, etc.). --- **C2. A private StreamElements widget access token is embedded directly in a browser-source URL inside the scene collection, and is duplicated into two backups.** - `C:\Users\Srini\AppData\Roaming\obs-studio\basic\scenes\Main.json:374` — a `browser_source`'s `"url"` is `https://widgets.streamelements.com/host//` — the trailing path segment is StreamElements' per-widget access token; anyone who has it can view/control that overlay widget's config. - Same URL, same token, duplicated verbatim in `C:\Users\Srini\obs-tools\backup-pre-agentselect-012817\Main.json` and `C:\Users\Srini\obs-backups\20261031-160039-baseline-pre-overhaul\basic\scenes\Main.json`. **Impact:** This is exactly the risk the review brief called out: a secret embedded in a browser-source URL is saved into the scene collection JSON. If that file is ever shared (scene-collection export/import to get help from someone, a GitHub gist of the "Main.json" for troubleshooting, a screen-share of OBS's Sources panel properties dialog which shows the full URL in a text field), the token leaks. It also means every backup of OBS silently carries a live credential forward forever. **Remediation:** 1. Regenerate the StreamElements widget URL/token from the StreamElements dashboard. 2. Where possible, prefer local overlay files (as the rest of this setup already does via the HUD server) over remote widget URLs that embed auth in the path. 3. Before sharing/exporting a scene collection or screenshotting Source Properties, scrub this field. --- ### HIGH **H1. The custom HUD server hands out the plaintext obs-websocket password over unauthenticated HTTP, to any process on the machine.** `C:\Users\Srini\obs-tools\obs-autopilot.py:1297-1300`: ```python if route == '/ws.json': return self._json({"host": "127.0.0.1", "port": cfg['port'], "password": cfg['password']}) ``` There is no authentication check on `do_GET`, and no token/origin check — any local process (or, in principle, any page that can reach `127.0.0.1:4466`, including a non-OBS browser tab doing a background request) can `GET /ws.json` and read the password back in cleartext JSON. The code comment at lines 1291-1296 correctly reasons that this is *no more exposed than the config file it reads from* because the server is loopback-bound — that reasoning is sound for the network dimension, but it does not account for **other local processes/malware reading from a well-known, unauthenticated local HTTP endpoint**, which is a materially easier target than finding and parsing a JSON config file on disk, and is also reachable from any Chromium-origin web page the user has open elsewhere (any site, not just OBS's own browser sources, since nothing here checks `Origin`/`Referer`). **Impact:** Any other software running as the same Windows user (or a browser tab that manages to probe this port) can trivially obtain the obs-websocket password without filesystem access, widening who/what can get it beyond "reads files in obs-tools." **Remediation:** Add a shared-secret header or `Origin` allow-list check on `/ws.json` (e.g. only serve it if `Origin` is `null`/`file://` or a known OBS-browser user agent string is present), or require a one-time token minted at autopilot startup and injected into the overlay HTML server-side instead of being fetchable by an arbitrary GET. **H2. obs-websocket's LAN exposure (see C1) combined with no Origin/CSWSH protection assessment.** obs-websocket is a closed-source compiled plugin (`obs-websocket.dll`); I could not inspect its source for Origin-header validation on the WebSocket handshake. What's confirmed is: it binds all interfaces (C1), and the WebSocket protocol does not get CORS preflight protection the way `fetch()` does. If obs-websocket does not validate `Origin`, then **any web page the user visits in their normal browser** — not just OBS browser sources — could attempt `new WebSocket('ws://192.168.0.4:4456')` or `ws://127.0.0.1:4456` from JavaScript; the only thing stopping it from succeeding is the password-based `authentication` challenge, which requires knowing the plaintext password already covered in C1. This is a DNS-rebinding-class risk if the password ever leaks: the attack surface is "connect from any page" rather than "connect from the local machine only." **Remediation:** Treat password secrecy (C1) as the only real control here, since the plugin offers no bind-address or Origin controls. Firewalling TCP 4456 from non-loopback sources (C1 remediation #4) removes the remote half of this risk; it does not remove the "malicious page open in the user's own browser" half, which again comes back to not leaking the password (C1, H1). **H3. Risk from StreamElements/other-widget session cookies swept into every backup.** `C:\Users\Srini\AppData\Roaming\obs-studio\plugin_config\obs-browser\Network\Cookies` is a live Chromium cookie database for the embedded browser-source engine, encrypted at rest via Windows DPAPI (`LocalPrefs.json` shows an `os_crypt.encrypted_key` entry). `backup-obs.ps1:14` copies the entire `plugin_config` tree, including this database, into every backup. DPAPI ties the encryption to this Windows user profile, so the practical risk is low as long as backups stay on this machine under this account — but if a backup is ever moved to another machine/profile (cloud sync, USB transfer "for safekeeping"), the cookie values become unrecoverable garbage (not a security hole) while still being dead weight; more importantly, if an attacker already has code execution as this Windows user, the DPAPI protection is moot and these cookies (for streamelements.com and anything else a browser source ever visited) are exposed same as any other secret here. **Remediation:** Informational — no action required unless backups leave this machine/account. If they do, exclude `plugin_config\obs-browser\Network\Cookies*` and `Local Storage` from the backup, or explicitly accept that risk. --- ### MEDIUM **M1. Twitch IRC `color` tag is concatenated into an HTML `style` attribute without escaping.** `C:\Users\Srini\obs-overlays\chatbox.html:169`: ```js '' + esc(name) + '' ``` `color` is `tags.color` from the raw Twitch IRC tags (`chatbox.html:216`), and unlike the message body (`esc()` used, see M-info below) and the display name (`esc(name)`), it is **not** passed through `esc()` before being spliced into an HTML attribute. Twitch's server is expected to only ever send a `#rrggbb` hex value or an empty string for this tag, so exploitation requires either a bug/compromise on Twitch's IRC-tag validation or a modified/relay client sending a crafted tag value — but the page has no defense of its own if that assumption is ever violated. A crafted value containing a `"` could close the `style` attribute early and inject arbitrary attributes/markup into a source that is live on stream. **Impact (if the upstream assumption fails):** XSS/markup injection into a visible, on-stream overlay. **Remediation:** Escape `color` the same way `name` and the message body are escaped (`esc(color)`), or validate it against `/^#[0-9a-f]{6}$/i` and fall back to `pickColor(name)` otherwise. Trivial, low-risk fix; do it regardless of how likely the upstream bug is. **M1-info (verified safe).** The chat message body itself IS correctly escaped before being placed into `innerHTML`: `twitchBody()` (`chatbox.html:234-257`) runs every text segment through `esc()` (`chatbox.html:156-157`, escapes `& < > "`) both around and between emote `` substitutions, and the display name is escaped at `chatbox.html:169` via `esc(name)`. This is the one part of the review brief ("a chatbox rendering untrusted viewer chat via innerHTML is a real risk") that was checked carefully and found to be implemented correctly, aside from the `color` attribute gap above. **M2. YouTube Data API key is designed to travel through the browser-source URL (architectural gap, not currently exploited).** `C:\Users\Srini\obs-overlays\chatbox.html:338,342`: ```js const tw = Q.get('twitch'), ytKey = Q.get('yt_key'), ytVid = Q.get('yt_video'); ... if (ytKey && ytVid) startYouTube(ytKey, ytVid); ``` The YouTube Data API key is read straight from the OBS browser-source URL query string (`?yt_key=...`), which — exactly like C2 — gets written verbatim into the scene collection JSON and into every properties-dialog view/screenshot. **This is not currently exploited**: `yt_key`/`yt_video` do not appear anywhere in `Main.json`, so the YouTube chat path is not configured today. But the design means the moment someone configures it, the key is in the scene collection in plaintext, with no equivalent to the HUD-server indirection that `obs-meter.js` uses for the obs-websocket password. **Remediation:** Route the YouTube key the same way `obs-meter.js` routes the obs-websocket password — serve it from `/ws.json`-style endpoint on the already-loopback-bound HUD server, keyed off `autopilot.config.json`, instead of a URL query parameter. **M3. Valorant PUUID + Riot ID stored in `identity.json`, and used with TLS verification disabled.** - `C:\Users\Srini\obs-tools\identity.json` — contains a durable Riot `puuid` and Riot ID (`name#tag`). This is not a password, but a PUUID is a stable, reusable identifier that (with the right Riot API access) can be used to pull match history/rank; the Riot ID is directly searchable in-game. - Verified the PUUID/name is **not** rendered into any overlay HTML and is not broadcast on stream (checked all of `obs-overlays/*.html` for `identity`/`puuid`/`riot` — no matches); it's only consumed internally by `obs-autopilot.py` to match "me" in match data (`obs-autopilot.py:879-908`). The HUD server that exposes derived state is loopback-only (see Network section). - `obs-autopilot.py:688-692` disables TLS verification (`check_hostname = False`, `verify_mode = ssl.CERT_NONE`) when talking to Riot's local client API. This is the standard, necessary workaround for Riot's self-signed local certificate and the target is always `127.0.0.1` (`obs-autopilot.py:698`), so it is not itself exploitable remotely — flagged here only for completeness, not as an action item. **Impact:** Low on its own (not broadcast, loopback-only consumption); becomes Medium only in combination with C1/H1, since `identity.json` sits in the same directory and backups as the password and gets swept into the same backup copies. **Remediation:** No urgent action; if `obs-tools` is ever made shareable (e.g. put in a public git repo), exclude `identity.json` same as the config file. **M4. `obs-backgroundremoval` is listed as an installed plugin but has no corresponding DLL under `C:\Program Files\obs-studio\obs-plugins\64bit\`.** Its plugin-config folder exists (`AppData\Roaming\obs-studio\plugin_config\obs-backgroundremoval\`), and it was copied into the baseline backup, but no `*background*`/`*remov*`-named `.dll` exists anywhere under `C:\Program Files\obs-studio\` (checked recursively). Either the plugin was uninstalled without its config being cleaned up, or it is not actually providing background removal today (NVIDIA's bundled `nv-filters.dll`, which IS present and signed by OBS Project, may be covering that use case instead). This is a functionality/provenance gap, not a security hole — flagged so the plugin inventory used for planning matches reality. **Remediation:** Confirm whether background removal is expected to work; if the plugin is gone, delete its orphaned config folder; if it's expected, reinstall it and re-run the signature check below. --- ### LOW **L1. `input-overlay`'s WebSocket server is configured to bind `0.0.0.0` (latent, currently disabled).** `C:\Users\Srini\AppData\Roaming\obs-studio\global.ini`, `[input-overlay]` section: ``` wss_address=0.0.0.0 wss_port=16899 enable_wss=false ``` `enable_wss=false`, so this is not currently listening — but if a future "enable remote input display" toggle is flipped, it will bind to all interfaces by default. Note also that the bundled preset `input-overlay-presets-510\input-history-windows\input-history-windows.html:1059` connects to `ws://localhost:16899/`, consistent with this being meant for local use only; there's no reason the server itself needs `0.0.0.0`. **Remediation:** Change `wss_address` to `127.0.0.1` now, while it's inert, so a future "turn it on" doesn't silently reopen a LAN-facing port. **L2. `autopilot-launcher.lua:27` uses `os.execute()` with string-concatenated, double-quoted paths.** ```lua os.execute('start "" "' .. PYTHONW .. '" "' .. AUTOPILOT .. '"') ``` Both `PYTHONW` and `AUTOPILOT` are hardcoded constants in the same file (lines 15-16), not derived from any external/untrusted input, so there is no injection vector today. Flagged only because the pattern (building a shell command by string concatenation) is fragile — if either path constant is ever parameterized from OBS script settings or an environment variable, this becomes an injection point. No action required unless the script is changed to take configurable paths. **L3. No other `shell=True`, `os.system`, `eval`, or `exec` usage found.** Searched every `.py` file in `obs-tools\` (`add_input_overlay.py`, `add_overlays.py`, `audit-audio.py`, `audit-full-files.py`, `audit-full.py`, `audit.py`, `layout.py`, `layout_inputs.py`, `migrate-drop-agent-select.py`, `obs-autopilot.py`, `rename_scenes.py`, `scan_orphans.py`, `sharpen_overlays.py`) for `subprocess`, `os.system`, `shell=True`, `eval(`, `exec(`, `os.popen`. The only `subprocess.run` call (`audit-full-files.py:112`) passes a list of literal arguments (no `shell=True`) and takes no runtime/untrusted input — safe. No path-traversal issues found in file writes; all file paths written by `obs-autopilot.py` (`autopilot.config.json`, `identity.json`, daily-stats JSON, clip log, Minecraft stats) are built from fixed constants (`HERE`, `os.path.join`) or from the Minecraft log path derived from `%LOCALAPPDATA%`/`.minecraft` conventions in `_mc_log_path(cfg)`, not from untrusted network input. --- ## Network Service Audit — Definitive Answers | Service | Configured/intended | Actual bind, as evidenced | Verdict | |---|---|---|---| | OBS WebSocket (obs-websocket) | `autopilot.config.json` dials `127.0.0.1:4456` | OBS log, `2026-10-31 01-34-10.txt`: *"Not locked to IPv4 bindings"* / *"Possible connect address: 192.168.0.4"* on port 4456 | **LAN-exposed.** obs-websocket always binds all interfaces; there is no bind-address setting in its config.json or UI. `auth_required: true` + `server_password` set (plugin_config\obs-websocket\config.json) is the only control. | | Custom HUD HTTP server (obs-autopilot.py, port 4466) | — | `obs-autopilot.py:1315`: `srv = ThreadingHTTPServer(('127.0.0.1', cfg['hud_port']), Handler)` | **Loopback-only, by explicit code.** Confirmed directly from source — the bind tuple is hardcoded to `'127.0.0.1'`. | Neither service was running at the time of this review (`tasklist` showed no `obs64.exe`/`pythonw.exe`, and `netstat -ano | findstr LISTENING` showed nothing on 4456/4466), so live-port verification wasn't possible; the above is based on source code (HUD server) and the most recent OBS session's own startup log (obs-websocket), which is first-party evidence of actual bind behavior, not speculation. Other listening ports found via `netstat -ano | findstr LISTENING` at review time: standard Windows services only (135/445 RPC/SMB, ephemeral 49664-49671 RPC, 192.168.0.4:139 NetBIOS) plus two unrelated loopback services on 9010/9180/45654 (PID 12264/3340 — not identified as streaming-related, likely a background app; out of scope but noted in case the lead wants to check PID 12264/3340 ownership). Nothing streaming-related was listening because nothing was running. **Is there authentication on the HUD server?** No. `do_GET` (obs-autopilot.py:1287-1301) serves `/state.json` and `/ws.json` to any caller with no check at all. `/ws.json` returns the obs-websocket password in cleartext (H1). Input validation is minimal: the only dynamic routing is `self.path.split('?')[0]` string comparison against two literal routes, falling through to `SimpleHTTPRequestHandler`'s static file serving (which itself guards against `..` path traversal as part of Python's stdlib) for everything else — no user-controlled path construction was found. **Could a malicious page reach these via CSRF/DNS rebinding?** For the HUD server: a cross-origin page can send a GET to `/ws.json` (no preflight needed), and while it cannot *read* the JSON response due to lack of CORS headers (the browser treats it as an opaque response), this does not fully rule out side-channel leakage and does nothing to stop a page that IS same-origin (any OBS browser source) or a local process. For obs-websocket: see H2 — the real protection is password secrecy, not network topology, since the plugin binds all interfaces and WebSocket connections aren't subject to the same-origin/CORS model fetch() uses. --- ## Code Review — Injection & Unsafe Execution Reviewed: `obs-autopilot.py`, `autopilot-launcher.lua`, `add_overlays.py`, `layout.py`, plus every other `.py` in `obs-tools\`. - **No** `subprocess(..., shell=True)`, **no** `os.system`, **no** `eval(`/`exec(` found anywhere in the reviewed scripts (L3 above has the full file list and detail). - **No** command built from untrusted HTTP-response or Valorant-local-API data. # Besecstasy#GOSTジ — Gotham Broadcast Overhaul: Creative Concepts

Prepared as design work only. No file in `obs-overlays/` or the OBS scene collection was modified to produce this document. Scene/source names below were cross-checked against the live collection at `C:\Users\Srini\AppData\Roaming\obs-studio\basic\scenes\Main.json` (read-only) so the naming is exact, not guessed.

---

## 1. Visual Identity Assessment

### What's genuinely strong — preserve this, don't touch it

**The palette discipline is the single best asset in this build.** `gotham.css` states the rule explicitly and the rest of the codebase actually obeys it: every colour is sampled from the emblem — black, burnt orange, amber, gold, brass — and the comment calls out, correctly, that a "neutral" grey with its blue channel highest reads as blue on a dark ground. `scoreboard.html` even has an inline comment fixing exactly that bug (`--accent2 ... was a cool steel`). This is a team that already caught and corrected its own cool-tint drift once. Any new overlay must pass the same test: sample from the emblem, vary by value/tint only, never by hue.

**The chrome-bevel + ink-panel system (`.chrome`, `.panel`) is reused everywhere** — `chatbox.html`, `titlebar.html`, `screens.html` — via one shared gradient recipe (padded gradient, not border-image, so the corner radius and highlight track together). That's a real design system, not copy-pasted CSS. New overlays should extend `.chrome`, not invent a second frame language.

**The spotlight/fog/rain/grain primitives read as one cinematic language**, and they're built cheaply: CSS gradients and `repeating-linear-gradient`, no video textures, no canvas. `screens.html`'s 3D-spun emblem (`#spin`, `.face.front/.back`, the Z-stacked `.slice` extrusion) is a genuinely impressive touch for pure CSS — a licensed 2D logo reads as a machined medallion rotating in space, lit by a `--lit` custom property keyed to the same timeline as the spin. This is above the bar for "just an overlay."

**`obs-meter.js` is architecturally correct.** It pulls real levels from OBS's own obs-websocket meters rather than doing browser-side audio capture (which browser sources can't do anyway), degrades silently to `--glow: 0` if the socket never connects, and resolves its password from the autopilot's `/ws.json` instead of embedding a credential in every browser-source URL (which would otherwise get saved in cleartext into the scene collection). Every reactive surface — title bar, screens, cam frame, chat accent — reads off one `--glow` value set on `<html>`. One signal, many consumers. That's the right pattern for all future audio-reactive work.

**`stinger.html`'s timing model is the most technically careful file in the set.** The comment block explaining *why* the animation (`?ms=2000`) is deliberately shorter than the transition duration (2600ms) — to absorb browser-source reload latency as "tail" slack after the visual is already fully transparent — shows real production debugging, not guesswork. The asymmetric intro/outro (soft shutter-close vs. hard snap-open with a light-streak bleed) is a genuine piece of motion design. Nobody should "simplify" this file without re-reading that comment first.

**The naming convention (`CAP-/CAM-/HUD-/IN-/FX-/AUD-/ALR-/SCR-/GRP-`) is followed with zero exceptions** across all 33 sources in the live collection. This alone makes the whole rig legible at a glance in the OBS source list, and it's the thing most streamers never bother to do. Every proposal below keeps it intact.

**Minecraft gets a genuinely separate visual language (`minecraft.html`) rather than a recolour** — hard pixel grid, stepped-block border via `repeating-linear-gradient` conic steps, corner torches with per-torch flicker offsets so they never pulse in sync, embers that respect the game's own safe-area (bottom-centre hotbar, bottom-left chat are explicitly left untouched). That safe-area discipline is also why the crosshair is correctly left alone — it's a precision tool, not decoration, and the existing rig already treats the game's own UI as sacred ground to design around rather than over.

**Per-game accent variables (`[data-accent="valorant"]`, `"finals"`, `"solo"`) stay inside the same hue family** and differ only by value/tint — `titlebar.html`, `chatbox.html`, `screens.html`, `reactive.html` all implement this identically. Consistent, extensible, and it means a fifth game (GeoGuessr, iRacing) is a four-line CSS addition, not a redesign.

### What's dated or inconsistent

- **No accent exists yet for GeoGuessr or iRacing.** The `[data-accent]` pattern is ready for them but nobody's written the two extra rules. Trivial to fix, flagged here so it doesn't get missed when those games actually get scenes.
- **The licensed-emblem fallback chain is duplicated by hand in six different files** (`stinger.html`, `screens.html`, `titlebar.html`, `reactive.html`, `cam-bg.html`, `overlay.html`) — each one reimplements the same `img.onerror` cascade over `['assets/emblem.svg', 'assets/emblem.png', 'assets/emblem-fallback.svg']`. It works, but it's the one piece of real duplication in an otherwise disciplined codebase, and a future emblem-path change means editing six files instead of one. Not urgent, but worth a shared tiny `emblem.js` eventually.
- **`scoreboard.html` has no `<link rel="stylesheet" href="gotham.css">`** — it reimplements its own `:root` palette, its own font-face, its own body reset. It still lands in the right palette by hand, but it's drifted out of the shared system syntactically (it even redefines `--bat`/`--ink`/`--bone`, which `gotham.css` already defines identically). Low risk today because the values match, but it's the one file that would silently diverge if the shared palette ever changed.
- **Three stale `.pre-*` backup files sit in the live folder** (`minecraft.html.pre-margin`, `overlay.html.pre-margin`, `screens.html.pre-margin`, `scoreboard.html.pre-finalsremove`). Harmless as long as nothing references them, but worth clearing out during any housekeeping pass so a future editor doesn't accidentally open the wrong one.
- **`overlay.html`'s vignette/watermark layer and `minecraft.html`'s theme layer are two separate "ambient shading" systems that never talk to each other** — a scene with both active (none currently does) would need care about z-order and double-darkening. Not a bug today, just a seam to be aware of before anything gets layered.
- **The emblem's licensed artwork is explicitly NOT present** per `assets/README.md`'s own description (it describes what *would* be dropped in) — the system is designed to run entirely on `emblem-fallback.svg` and the CSS-only skyline fallback. That's a legitimate design decision (licensed art stays local-only, never shipped), but it does mean the "signature" element of the identity right now is the drawn fallback bat, not licensed art. Worth confirming that's intentional and permanent vs. a placeholder waiting on an asset drop.

### What's missing

- **No Competitive/Just-Chatting/Cinematic/Recording/Emergency-Fallback scene variants** — only game-specific scenes (`1 - Gaming`, `2 - Minecraft`) plus the three screen states and the alert/stinger scenes exist today. That's Task 4 below.
- **No GeoGuessr or iRacing capture/HUD sources at all** — content the streamer plays regularly has zero overlay support right now.
- **No clip/highlight pipeline** — `source-record` is available but unused in the collection; nothing currently isolates game capture for post-stream editing.
- **No viewer-facing audience-interaction surface beyond `ALR - StreamElements`** — no in-house alert styling that matches the chrome/amber language as tightly as the rest of the rig (StreamElements alerts are presumably still in that service's default skin, not Gotham-skinned).
- **No use of `downstream-keyer`, `backgroundremoval`, `source-clone` beyond the one `CAM - Ambient Glow` clone, `input-overlay` beyond keyboard/mouse, or `obs-shaderfilter` anywhere** — half the installed plugin roster is idle. That's not a flaw, it's headroom; several concepts below spend it.

**crosshair.html was not opened for editing and no change is proposed to it anywhere in this document** — confirmed untouched, per instruction.

---

## 2. Concept Bank (34 concepts, 8 categories)

Scoring key (1–10, Difficulty inverted: 10 = hardest):
`Orig` Originality · `Eng` Viewer Engagement · `Use` Practical Usefulness · `PerfEff` Performance Efficiency (10 = cheapest) · `Diff` Implementation Difficulty (10 = hardest)

### A. Visual

**A1. Round-Outcome Spotlight Flare (full-capture)**
Extends the round `#flare` pulse already coded into `scoreboard.html` from a HUD strip accent into a brief full-screen amber/signal-gold wash over the whole canvas on round win/loss, reusing the same `doFlare(who)` colour logic.
- Viewer sees: a half-second warm or cold light wash across the entire frame at the instant a Valorant round is won or lost — readable even with sound off.
- Implementation: new `FX - Round Flare (Full)` browser source, full-canvas, placed above `CAP - Valorant` and below HUD strips in `1 - Gaming`; driven by the same `/state.json` `round.at`/`round.who` fields the HUD strip already polls, so autopilot needs zero new code.
- Required software: none beyond what's installed.
- Custom dev needed: small (one new HTML file, ~60 lines, copy the flare keyframes out of `scoreboard.html`).
- Hardware overhead: ~0.5–1% GPU, only during the ~1.5s animation window; a CSS radial-gradient opacity fade, no shaders.
- Complexity: Low. Security: none (reads only local `/state.json`, no new network surface).
- Priority: High.
- Scores: Orig 5, Eng 7, Use 7, PerfEff 10, Diff 2.

**A2. Weather-by-Performance (reactive rain density)**
Ties the existing `.rain`/`.fog` opacity in `gotham.css` to live K/D from `/state.json` instead of a fixed constant — rain gets heavier as the session's K/D worsens, thins out on a hot streak.
- Viewer sees: the ambient Gotham rain subtly intensifying during a rough match and clearing during a win streak — an atmospheric scoreline nobody has to read as text.
- Implementation: a small poll script added only to scenes that already include `.rain`/`.fog` (currently none visibly do outside `screens.html`'s BRB/Starting Soon cards) — more realistically ship this as an optional variant of A1/A3 rather than a new source.
- Required software: none. Custom dev: small (pure JS fetch loop + CSS variable set).
- Hardware overhead: negligible, <0.5% CPU for a 1s-interval fetch.
- Complexity: Low. Security: none.
- Priority: Medium — nice texture, but it's a subtlety easy to miss live; pair with A1, don't ship standalone.
- Scores: Orig 6, Eng 5, Use 4, PerfEff 10, Diff 2.

**A3. Searchlight Sweep (idle BRB/Starting Soon variant)**
Replaces the static breathing spotlight in `screens.html` with an occasional slow sweep across the card during long BRB/Starting-Soon holds, so the screen doesn't look frozen on a 10-minute break.
- Viewer sees: the spotlight cone slowly arcing side to side every 20–30s instead of sitting still.
- Implementation: extend `.spotlight`'s existing `gothamBreathe` keyframe with an additional `translate`/rotate pass; pure CSS, same `SCR - BRB` / `SCR - Starting Soon` sources.
- Required software: none. Custom dev: small (CSS-only edit).
- Hardware overhead: negligible — same element, same compositing cost as today.
- Complexity: Low. Security: none.
- Priority: Medium.
- Scores: Orig 4, Eng 5, Use 5, PerfEff 10, Diff 1.

**A4. Flash/Damage Glitch Pass (shaderfilter)**
A one-shot chromatic-aberration/glitch pulse on the cam frame when autopilot detects the player got flashed in Valorant (state already tracked for match polling can be extended to ability events if the API exposes them; if not, trigger on round-loss only as a safe substitute).
- Viewer sees: the cam frame glitches briefly in sync with getting flashed — a reaction-shot gag that reads instantly on clips.
- Implementation: `obs-shaderfilter` on `CAM - Frame`, enabled/disabled via `obs-websocket` `SetSourceFilterEnabled` from autopilot.
- Required software: obs-shaderfilter (installed).
- Custom dev: medium — needs autopilot to expose a flash/ability event, which may not exist in the current match-state poll; verify before committing to the flash trigger specifically.
- Hardware overhead: ~2–4% GPU, but only during the ~300ms pulse, not continuous.
- Complexity: Medium. Security: none (local filter toggle only).
- Priority: Medium — compelling but gated on an autopilot feature that may not exist yet.
- Scores: Orig 7, Eng 7, Use 4, PerfEff 8, Diff 5.

**A5. IRL/Variety Day Weather Toggle**
Packages the existing `.rain`/`.fog`/`.grain` classes as an explicit optional layer any new "Cinematic" or IRL-adjacent scene can turn on/off per occasion (e.g., a rainy real-world day, a moodier VOD review session) without writing new CSS.
- Viewer sees: the signature Gotham weather applied consistently to non-gameplay scenes when the streamer wants the mood, not just BRB/Starting Soon.
- Implementation: no new code — just a documented convention of including the existing classes in new `SCR-`/`FX-` sources.
- Required software: none. Custom dev: none (reuse only).
- Hardware overhead: same as current rain/fog (already proven cheap).
- Complexity: Trivial. Security: none.
- Priority: Low — it's already possible, just flagged so Cinematic Mode (Task 4) reuses it deliberately.
- Scores: Orig 2, Eng 4, Use 5, PerfEff 10, Diff 1.

### B. Gameplay

**B1. Rank-Delta Progress Bar**
Adds an RR-gain/loss progress bar under the existing `Rank` cell in `HUD - Minecraft Run`'s sibling for Valorant — i.e., extends `HUD - Mic Bars`'s neighbour, the match strip in `scoreboard.html`, with a thin bar showing progress toward rank-up, sourced from the same official rank string already polled.
- Viewer sees: a small amber-fill bar ticking up toward the next rank alongside the existing Rank text.
- Implementation: edit `scoreboard.html`'s `.cell` for rank to add a `<div class="bar">` filled via a new `/state.json` field (`rr_progress`), which autopilot computes from its existing rank polling.
- Required software: none new. Custom dev: small (one HTML/CSS addition + one autopilot field).
- Hardware overhead: negligible — same polling loop, one more DOM node.
- Complexity: Low. Security: none.
- Priority: High.
- Scores: Orig 4, Eng 6, Use 8, PerfEff 10, Diff 3.

**B2. Minecraft Boss-Fight Timer**
Extends `mc-hud.html`'s log-tailing approach (already reading `latest.log` for deaths/advancements with no mod required) to flag known boss-encounter log lines (Ender Dragon perch, Wither summon) and show an elapsed fight timer row.
- Viewer sees: a new "Boss Fight: 1:42" row appears the moment a dragon/wither fight starts, ticking live.
- Implementation: new row in `HUD - Minecraft Run`, fed by an autopilot log-pattern addition; follows the existing `.row`/`.k`/`.v` block style exactly.
- Required software: none new. Custom dev: medium (autopilot needs new log-pattern matching; the overlay-side change is small).
- Hardware overhead: negligible — log tailing is already happening.
- Complexity: Medium. Security: none (local file read only).
- Priority: Medium.
- Scores: Orig 6, Eng 6, Use 5, PerfEff 10, Diff 4.

**B3. GeoGuessr Round HUD**
A small `HUD - GeoGuessr Round` strip showing round timer and last-guess distance, fed not by memory-reading (GeoGuessr has no local process to read) but by a tiny, purpose-built browser extension that reads the GeoGuessr tab's own DOM and posts JSON to autopilot's existing local HTTP server.
- Viewer sees: round countdown and "last guess: 340km off" distance readout styled identically to the Valorant match strip.
- Implementation: new `CAP - GeoGuessr` (window/display capture of the browser tab) + `HUD - GeoGuessr Round` browser source; a small unpacked Chrome/Firefox extension (content script + `fetch` POST) is the only new "software."
- Required software: a hand-written browser extension (not a game mod, not memory access — DOM scraping of a website you're voluntarily browsing). No anti-cheat exposure since GeoGuessr has none.
- Custom dev: medium (extension + one new HUD page + one new autopilot endpoint).
- Hardware overhead: negligible — extension runs inside the browser you already have open; no extra GPU render pass beyond a normal `HUD-` browser source.
- Complexity: Medium. Security: a content script with host permissions on geoguessr.com only — scoped narrowly, reviewed before install, zero other sites touched. **Flag for approval**: new third-party-adjacent code (a browser extension) running with page access, even scoped.
- Priority: Medium-High — content you play regularly with zero current overlay support.
- Scores: Orig 8, Eng 7, Use 7, PerfEff 9, Diff 5.

**B4. iRacing Telemetry Strip**
A `HUD - iRacing Telemetry` bar (speed/gear/lap-delta) using iRacing's own official shared-memory telemetry SDK — a first-party, intentionally-exposed read API, not memory injection, not anything Vanguard-equivalent would flag (iRacing has no comparable kernel anti-cheat and explicitly documents this interface for exactly this use).
- Viewer sees: live speed, gear, and lap delta styled with the same chrome-bevel HUD language as the Valorant strip.
- Implementation: a small Python or C# bridge reading iRacing's shared memory block, writing it into the same `state.json` shape autopilot already produces, consumed by a new HTML HUD styled off `scoreboard.html`.
- Required software: `pyirsdk` (or equivalent) — a well-established, iRacing-sanctioned library.
- Custom dev: medium (bridge script + one HUD page).
- Hardware overhead: negligible — a background Python process polling shared memory at low frequency, well under 1% CPU.
- Complexity: Medium. Security: none (local shared memory, no network, no injection).
- Priority: Medium — real but lower-frequency content than Valorant/Minecraft; build once the higher-priority items land.
- Scores: Orig 6, Eng 6, Use 7, PerfEff 9, Diff 5.

### C. Audience Interaction

**C1. Redeem-Triggered Mini Bat-Signal**
A shortened variant of `stinger.html` (`?ms=700` instead of 2000) fired as a brief non-transition overlay flash on big cheer/sub events, without swapping scenes — just the shutter-and-emblem flash layered momentarily over whatever scene is live.
- Viewer sees: the bat emblem flares briefly over the current scene on a big sub/bits event, distinct from the full scene-change stinger.
- Implementation: `Streamer.bot` action → `obs-websocket` → show/hide a dedicated `FX - Mini Signal` browser source (same HTML as `stinger.html` with `restart_when_active` so it replays on every show).
- Required software: Streamer.bot (listed as "soon"). Custom dev: small (reuse existing stinger HTML with different params).
- Hardware overhead: ~1–2% GPU for well under a second, matching the existing stinger's cost profile.

## 4. Recommended Shortlist (ranked)

**Curation principle:** favor concepts that extend infrastructure already proven in this codebase (`/state.json` polling, `obs-meter.js`'s `--glow` pipeline, the `.chrome`/`.amber-text` CSS system, autopilot's event detection) over anything requiring a new standing service, a new input surface from strangers, or GPU budget that competes with Valorant frame time.

1. **C3 — Case File Shoutout Card.** Fixes the one visibly off-brand element in the current live rig (`ALR - StreamElements`'s default skin) with real viewer-facing payoff every follow/raid. High usefulness, reuses existing plugin (downstream-keyer) that's installed and currently idle.
2. **D3 — Automated Health-Triggered Fallback.** Directly protects the hardware-ceiling priority stated in the brief: if frames start dropping, the stream gets *lighter*, automatically, instead of staying on an overloaded scene until a human notices. This is the single highest-leverage reliability concept here.
3. **D2 — Clip-Worthy Moment Auto-Flagging.** Near-zero live cost (it's a background logging change), unlocks F1 for free, and turns "editing the VOD" from a scrubbing chore into a markers list.
4. **A1 — Round-Outcome Spotlight Flare.** Cheapest possible visual payoff (reuses existing flare logic from `scoreboard.html` almost verbatim) with real engagement value — readable with sound off, which matters for clips.
5. **E2 — Round-Outcome Audio Stabs.** Ship alongside A1; same trigger, same event, doubles the signature-moment payoff for almost no extra work.
6. **B1 — Rank-Delta Progress Bar.** Small, cheap, genuinely useful — the kind of HUD improvement that compounds every single competitive session rather than a one-off gag.
7. **C1 — Redeem-Triggered Mini Bat-Signal.** The strongest "this stream has a signature move" audience-interaction idea in the bank, and it's a parameter variant of a file that already exists and already works (`stinger.html`).
8. **C2 — Chat-Voted BRB Accent.** Cheap, funny, directly reuses the `[data-accent]` system that's already built into three files — this is "spend five minutes of chat's attention on a feature we basically already have."
9. **G1 — Rogues Gallery Top-Chatter Card.** The best community-recognition idea for the lowest build cost; meaningfully different from a generic leaderboard widget because it's styled in-identity.
10. **F1 — Auto-Compiled Highlight Reel.** Pure payoff once D2 exists; zero live-stream risk since it runs entirely post-stream.
11. **D1 — Smoother Auto-Switch Transitions.** Likely near-zero additional work (may already be close to working via the existing `Move` transition) for a real polish gain on every single automatic scene change.
12. **B3 — GeoGuessr Round HUD.** The strongest "fills an actual content gap" pick — GeoGuessr currently has zero overlay support despite being regular content — but ranked last because it needs a small custom browser extension (new, narrow, but real attack surface) and should get explicit sign-off before building, not quiet default-yes treatment like the rest of this list.

### Explicitly NOT worth building (and why)

- **F3 — Clutch Replay Inset.** The idea is good (instant corner-replay of a clutch) but it's the single worst performance-efficiency score in the whole bank (4/10) precisely because it demands a second simultaneous encode of the game capture via `source-clone`, on the hardware whose explicit top priority is Valorant frame time. This is the textbook case of a flashy feature that directly fights the stated constraint. Revisit only if a future GPU upgrade changes the budget math — don't build it on the 4060 Ti.
- **H4 — Evidence Board Corkboard.** Letting strangers push arbitrary images directly onto a live broadcast is a moderation and security problem first and a feature second. Even with an approval queue, it's a standing custom upload server (new network surface) for a novelty that a Discord channel already covers better and more safely. Not recommended at all, approval-gated or not.
- **H2 — Detective Vision Shader Pass.** Visually the most striking idea here, but it needs a hand-tuned shader running during exactly the moments (clutch rounds) when frame time matters most, and the only safe version of it ("never mid-combat, round-boundary only") sharply limits when it can actually fire — a lot of shader-dev effort for a narrow window of legal use. Worth a second look only after Competitive Mode's frame budget is proven comfortable with margin to spare.
- **E3 — Gotham Live Captions.** Accessibility value is real, but continuous local ASR is the single heaviest CPU item in this entire bank (8–15%) on a chip that's also running OBS's encode and the game. Fine for Just Chatting; not worth building as a priority item given it must be hard-gated off during the content (Valorant) the brief says matters most — the gating logic adds complexity for a feature that's then unavailable during primary content anyway.
- **H1 — Multistream Groundwork.** Not "bad," just explicitly out of scope — YouTube is deferred per the brief, so spending build time on multistream plumbing today is effort against a priority that doesn't exist yet. A 20-minute later-check is enough; it doesn't need a project slot now.
- **A2 — Weather-by-Performance** and **C4 — Fog/Rain Intensity Redeem** overlap heavily with each other and with A1/C2 respectively — both are real but neither earns a separate build slot; fold A2 into A1 as an optional variant, and pick C2 over C4 since accent-voting has more replay value than a one-shot intensity bump.

---

## 5. Broadcast Mode Specs

All five modes are new scenes, named and ordered per the existing convention. Sources marked **(existing)** are taken verbatim from the live `Main.json` collection; sources marked **(new)** need to be created, following the same naming prefix rules observed throughout the current collection.

### Competitive Mode — minimal, Valorant-only, FPS-first

**Scene name:** `1a - Competitive`

Reuses almost everything from `1 - Gaming` but strips every non-essential render pass to protect frame time, and removes the cam-card/input-overlay visual weight down to the smallest footprint that still shows mic status and match state.

Ordered source list (top = front):
1. `ALR - StreamElements` **(existing)** — alerts still need to reach the viewer even in competitive play.
2. `HUD - Mic Muted` **(existing)**
3. `HUD - Valorant Match` **(new)** — a slimmed, score-and-map-only variant of `scoreboard.html`'s `#bar`, with the season-stats panel (`#stats`) and round-flare (`#flare`) both disabled by default to keep this mode's render cost at the floor.
4. `CAM - Frame` **(existing)** — kept small/corner, no `CAM - Card` backdrop, no `CAM - Ambient Glow` clone (that's the one `source-clone` instance already in the collection — skip it here specifically because it's a second encode pass).
5. `CAM - Webcam` **(existing)**
6. `CAP - Valorant` **(existing)**, with `CAP - Valorant (Window Fallback)` **(existing)** behind it, unchanged.
7. `AUD - Game` / `AUD - Discord` / `AUD - Music (Spotify)` / `AUD - Music (Browser)` **(existing, all four)**
8. `FX - Rim (Mic)` **(existing)**

Explicitly dropped vs. `1 - Gaming`: `IN - Keyboard`, `IN - Mouse`, `GRP - Cam + Inputs`, `CAM - Card`, `CAM - Ambient Glow`. Input overlays are genuinely useful for coaching-style content but cost render time for information most competitive viewers don't need second-to-second; cut them here, keep them in `1 - Gaming` for non-ranked sessions.

Transition in/out: `Move` **(existing default)** for normal switches; `Bat Signal` (`scene_as_transition`, **existing**) only when entering/leaving the session, not between round states.

### Just Chatting Mode — large cam

**Scene name:** `6 - Just Chatting`

Cam becomes the primary subject; game capture is dropped entirely.

Ordered source list:
1. `ALR - Case File` **(new, from C3)** — or `ALR - StreamElements` **(existing)** if C3 hasn't been built yet.
2. `IN - Interrogation Queue` **(new, from C5)**
3. `HUD - Captions` **(new, from E3)** — the one mode where the ASR CPU cost is acceptable, per the assessment above.
4. `HUD - Goals` **(new, from G2)**
5. `CAM - Card` **(existing)** — resized large, centred, as the dominant frame instead of a corner element.
6. `CAM - Webcam` **(existing)**
7. `CAM - Frame` **(existing)**
8. `AUD - Discord` / `AUD - Music (Spotify)` / `AUD - Music (Browser)` **(existing)** — `AUD - Game` omitted since no game is running.
9. `FX - Rim (Mic)` **(existing)**

Transition: `Move` **(existing)** — the large-cam resize benefits visibly from `move-transition`'s interpolation rather than a hard cut.

### Cinematic Mode — mood/variety, atmosphere-forward

**Scene name:** `7 - Cinematic`

For VOD review, music sessions, or any segment where the Gotham atmosphere itself is the point rather than gameplay or chat density.

Ordered source list:
1. `FX - Weather (Cinematic)` **(new, packaging A5)** — the existing `.rain`/`.fog`/`.grain` classes from `gotham.css`, deliberately turned on as a full-scene layer rather than confined to the BRB/Starting-Soon cards.
2. `HUD - Mic Bars` **(existing)** — reused from the screen-state scenes rather than the full match strip; this mode isn't about live match data.
3. `CAM - Card` **(existing)**
4. `CAM - Webcam` **(existing)**
5. `CAM - Frame` **(existing)**
6. `AUD - Music (Spotify)` / `AUD - Music (Browser)` / `AUD - Discord` **(existing)**
7. `FX - Rim (Music)` **(existing)** — already the correct rim variant for non-mic-driven scenes, per its use in `3 - Starting Soon` / `4 - BRB` / `5 - Stream Ended`.

Transition: `Bat Signal` **(existing `scene_as_transition`)** on entry/exit, since Cinematic Mode is a deliberate mood shift the stinger is built for; `Move` for anything internal.

### Recording Mode — clean, no overlay, for off-platform capture

**Scene name:** `8 - Recording (Clean)`

For local recording intended for editing (tutorial footage, montage source, anything that shouldn't carry the on-stream HUD).

Ordered source list:
1. `CAM - Frame` **(existing)** — kept, since a clean recording of gameplay commentary still usually wants the cam.
2. `CAM - Webcam` **(existing)**
3. `CAP - Valorant` / `CAP - Minecraft` / `CAP - The Finals` / `CAP - Any Game` **(existing, whichever is active)**
4. `AUD - Game` / `AUD - Discord` (muted) / `AUD - Music (Spotify)` **(existing)**

Everything else — every `HUD -`, `ALR -`, `IN -`, `FX -` source — is deliberately absent. This is the one mode that is cheaper than every other mode in the document, by design: it exists specifically so `source-record`/replay-buffer captures used for later editing (feeding F1/F2) aren't burning render budget on overlay elements that get cropped out anyway.

Transition: `Cut` (no stinger, no move) — a recording-only scene has no viewer-facing transition moment to perform for.

### Emergency Fallback Mode — low overhead, known-good audio

**Scene name:** `9 - Fallback`

The automatic target for D3. Must render reliably even when the rest of the PC is under load — this is the scene that has to work when everything else is struggling, so it uses the fewest possible browser sources (each one is a Chromium process OBS has to keep live) and no `source-clone`/shader/ASR anywhere in it.

Ordered source list:
1. `SCR - BRB` **(existing)** — reused as-is; it's already the lightest full-screen card in the collection (no live match polling, just the static/animated screen).
2. `HUD - Mic Bars` **(existing)** — the only HUD element kept, since confirming audio is still alive is the one piece of information that matters most when something's gone wrong.
3. `AUD - Discord` **(existing)** — kept so the streamer can communicate with viewers/mods about what's happening even if game audio is the thing that broke.
4. `FX - Rim (Music)` **(existing)**

Everything else — all `CAP -`, `CAM -`, `IN -`, and match-polling `HUD -` sources — is dropped. `ALR - StreamElements` is also dropped here deliberately: if the stream is unstable enough to need the fallback, a new alert popping in is one more thing that can go wrong or distract from fixing the actual problem.

Transition: `Cut`, triggered programmatically by D3's `obs-websocket` call — a transition animation during a reliability incident is exactly the kind of thing that should not be competing for frame time. **This is the one mode-level item that needs streamer sign-off on specifics before autopilot is allowed to invoke it unattended**, per D3's note above: confirm the exact dropped-frame/render-lag threshold and the debounce window before wiring the auto-switch live.

---

## 6. Items Needing Explicit Approval Before Building

Flagged throughout, collected here for visibility:

- **D3 (Automated Health-Triggered Fallback)** — autonomous scene-switching needs the exact trigger threshold and debounce window confirmed by the streamer before it's allowed to act without a human in the loop.
- **B3 (GeoGuessr Round HUD)** — requires writing and installing a small custom browser extension with page access to geoguessr.com. Narrowly scoped and reviewable, but it's new third-party-adjacent code with host permissions, not just an OBS source — approve the extension's exact permission scope before installing.
- **H3 (Interrogation Room Alt-Angle)** — requires an actual hardware purchase (second camera), not just software/config.
- **H4 (Evidence Board Corkboard)** — not recommended at all, but if reconsidered later: never ship without a manual approval queue between upload and on-stream display; flagged as a hard requirement, not a suggestion.
- **C5 (Interrogation Q&A) / any chat-submitted-text surface** — must reuse `chatbox.html`'s existing `esc()` sanitization pattern before rendering any chat-submitted string as HTML; confirm this is actually wired in before launch, not just assumed.

# Plugin / App Research Matrix

Target environment: OBS Studio 32.2.2 (64-bit, standard install at `C:\Program Files\obs-studio`), Windows 11 Pro build 26200 x64.
Research date: 2026-10-31. Staging directory: `C:\Users\Srini\obs-staging\`.

**No installation was performed.** All files below were downloaded to staging only, hashed, and inspected by extracting to `C:\Users\Srini\obs-staging\_inspect\` (not to any OBS directory).

---

## Composite Blur (OBS plugin)

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Name | Composite Blur |
| Developer | FiniteSingularity |
| Official URL | https://github.com/FiniteSingularity/obs-composite-blur (releases: `/releases/latest`) |
| Latest Release | **v1.6.1** |
| Release Date | 2026-10-24 |
| Supported OBS Versions | Dual-track release. The **v1.6.0** release notes state explicitly: *"This release includes both the new OBS 33+ style plugin for Windows and Linux, as well as the OBS 30-32 style plugin. Download filenames denoted with Legacy if you are using OBS 30-32, and the non-Legacy if using OBS 33+."* `buildspec.json` pins a minimum OBS dependency of 30.0.0. |
| Windows Compat | **CRITICAL: for OBS 32.2.2 you must use the `-windows-legacy-x64` asset, NOT the plain `-windows-x64` asset.** The non-legacy build targets OBS 33+ plugin ABI and is not guaranteed compatible with 32.x. |
| Install Method | ZIP (manual copy) or MSI (GUI installer, not run per scope). Staged the ZIP. |
| Dependencies | OBS obs-deps 2023-11-03, Qt6 2023-11-03 (build-time only; no extra runtime install needed for a standard OBS 32 install, which already bundles its own Qt6/obs-deps). |
| Published Hash | SHA256 published in GitHub release notes body for every asset. `obs-composite-blur-1.6.1-windows-legacy-x64.zip` = `a8f2ada2a6223e4c0f28cc1add72892a90a1049c01de9c792970e5c6596d8dc9` |
| Computed SHA256 | `A8F2ADA2A6223E4C0F28CC1ADD72892A90A1049C01DE9C792970E5C6596D8DC9` |
| Hash Match | **MATCH** |
| Known Issues | Open GitHub issues are mostly macOS Metal renderer and Linux packaging issues (#137, #130, #38); one open issue (#104) about OBS WebSocket + Display Capture interaction causing a black source until the Filters dialog is opened — relevant to this environment since obs-websocket is already installed. No security advisories found. |
| File Manifest | See manifest table below. |
| Final Recommendation | Strongly Recommended (provided the legacy build is used) |
| Blocking Concerns | None, as long as the **legacy** asset is installed. Using the non-legacy `windows-x64.zip`/`.msi` on OBS 32.2.2 would be a compatibility blocker. |

### Composite Blur — File Manifest (from `obs-composite-blur-1.6.1-windows-legacy-x64.zip`)

Archive root contains a parent folder `obs-composite-blur\` (fixed in 1.6.1 specifically to correct a prior zip-structure bug), then:

```
obs-composite-blur\bin\64bit\obs-composite-blur.dll   -> OBS\obs-plugins\64bit\obs-composite-blur.dll
obs-composite-blur\bin\64bit\obs-composite-blur.pdb   -> OBS\obs-plugins\64bit\obs-composite-blur.pdb  (optional, debug symbols)
obs-composite-blur\data\manifest.json                 -> OBS\data\obs-plugins\obs-composite-blur\manifest.json
obs-composite-blur\data\locale\*.ini (5 files)         -> OBS\data\obs-plugins\obs-composite-blur\locale\
obs-composite-blur\data\shaders\*.effect (24 files)    -> OBS\data\obs-plugins\obs-composite-blur\shaders\
```
Note the extra nesting level (`obs-composite-blur\`) must be stripped — copy the contents of `bin\64bit\*` into `obs-plugins\64bit\`, and the contents of `data\*` into `data\obs-plugins\obs-composite-blur\`.

---

## Advanced Masks (OBS plugin)

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Name | Advanced Masks |
| Developer | FiniteSingularity |
| Official URL | https://github.com/FiniteSingularity/obs-advanced-masks ; also listed on OBS forum at https://obsproject.com/forum/resources/advanced-masks.1856/ (min. OBS version listed there: 28.0.0 — stale relative to the legacy/non-legacy split introduced in 1.6.0, see below) |
| Latest Release | **v1.6.1** |
| Release Date | 2026-10-24 |
| Supported OBS Versions | Same dual-track scheme as Composite Blur (same author/build pipeline): v1.6.0 was titled "OBS 33 Support" and added a parallel OBS-33+ build alongside the existing OBS 30-32 ("Legacy") build. |
| Windows Compat | **CRITICAL: for OBS 32.2.2, use `-windows-legacy-x64`, not the plain `-windows-x64` asset.** |
| Install Method | ZIP (manual copy) or MSI. Staged the ZIP. |
| Dependencies | Same OBS obs-deps/Qt6 build toolchain as Composite Blur; no extra runtime needed on a standard OBS 32 install. |
| Published Hash | SHA256 published in GitHub release notes for every asset. `obs-advanced-masks-1.6.1-windows-legacy-x64.zip` = `d26d862f099524ac5d5a5c1be5c43e9d89de2f30588ea5ab548bc3da2da9ee22` |
| Computed SHA256 | `D26D862F099524AC5D5A5C1BE5C43E9D89DE2F30588EA5AB548BC3DA2DA9EE22` |
| Hash Match | **MATCH** |
| Known Issues | 22 open issues at time of research; none are Windows/OBS-32-specific blockers. Notable: #102/#100/#51 HDR color-space/alpha handling bugs, #96 Adjustment Mask + Chroma Key interaction, #88 black screen after applying filter (unclear repro), #63 request for Windows code-signing/notarization (installer is currently unsigned — see below). No security advisories found. |
| File Manifest | See manifest table below. |
| Final Recommendation | Strongly Recommended (provided the legacy build is used) |
| Blocking Concerns | None, provided the legacy asset is installed. Flag: the Windows MSI/installer for this plugin is **not Authenticode-signed** (per open issue #63 requesting signing); this triggers a plain "unknown publisher" SmartScreen prompt on the MSI. Not a correctness blocker, just an expected warning — hash match confirms integrity regardless. |

### Advanced Masks — File Manifest (from `obs-advanced-masks-1.6.1-windows-legacy-x64.zip`)

Archive root has **no** parent folder (contents sit directly at zip root):

```
bin\64bit\obs-advanced-masks.dll   -> OBS\obs-plugins\64bit\obs-advanced-masks.dll
bin\64bit\obs-advanced-masks.pdb   -> OBS\obs-plugins\64bit\obs-advanced-masks.pdb  (optional, debug symbols)
data\manifest.json                 -> OBS\data\obs-plugins\obs-advanced-masks\manifest.json
data\locale\*.ini (3 files)         -> OBS\data\obs-plugins\obs-advanced-masks\locale\
data\shaders\*.effect (16 files)    -> OBS\data\obs-plugins\obs-advanced-masks\shaders\
```

## Streamer.bot (standalone app)

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Name | Streamer.bot |
| Developer | Streamer.bot (closed-source, official site streamer.bot) |
| Official URL | https://streamer.bot (downloads via `streamer.bot/downloads/releases/streamer.bot`, direct latest-stable link `streamer.bot/api/releases/streamer.bot/latest/download`) |
| Latest Release | **v1.0.7** (hotfix on top of v1.0.5/1.0.6; filename resolved from the signed download redirect was `Streamer.bot-x64-1.0.7.zip`) |
| Release Date | Not stated on a page WebFetch could reach without login (changelog page required auth to browse history fully); 1.0.7 is a recent hotfix per the official changelog (`streamer.bot/changelogs/v1.0.7`) — treat as current as of research date. |
| Supported OBS Versions | Not an OBS plugin — it is a standalone companion app that talks to OBS exclusively over **obs-websocket** (already installed in this environment per the pre-verified plugin list). Any OBS version exposing a working obs-websocket v5 interface is sufficient; OBS 32.2.2 with the existing obs-websocket plugin qualifies. |
| Windows Compat | Windows x64, portable (no installer, no admin rights needed — admin mode is explicitly discouraged by the docs). Confirmed this build is a genuine Windows executable with a valid Authenticode signature (see below). |
| Install Method | Not applicable to OBS directories at all — portable app meant to be extracted to its own folder (docs warn against OneDrive/Google Drive-synced folders) and run as `Streamer.bot.exe`. Nothing from this archive is copied into `C:\Program Files\obs-studio`. |
| Dependencies | Self-contained (148 files including its own ASP.NET Core/Kestrel, gRPC, LiteDB, and third-party integration DLLs bundled in the zip). No separate .NET runtime install documented as required. |
| Published Hash | **None published on the official site for this file.** Download is served via a time-limited, pre-signed Cloudflare R2 URL; no SHA256/MD5 is shown on the download or changelog pages. |
| Computed SHA256 | `47A4E56F7A8A3E5F09EC16A5BA14C50E034DD98D67D2DC1EC89A671994C1F5C5` (of the downloaded zip as a whole; no official value exists to compare against) |

This is a reasonable substitute for a published checksum but is **not** the same guarantee — flagging per instructions. |
| Known Issues | Per official 1.0.5→1.0.7 changelog: this was a hotfix chain driven by a login/update-check bug and a Twitch IRC→EventSub migration; no outstanding critical/security advisory found in the search done here. Twitch chat handling changed from IRC to EventSub as of 1.0.5 — a **behavior change**, not a bug, but worth knowing if any existing automations assume IRC. |

| Final Recommendation | Optional (it is a well-regarded, widely used companion app, but it is not an OBS plugin, has no published checksum, and its install step is outside OBS entirely — final call on where to place the portable folder is a decision for the lead/installer, not this research step) |

No explicit "last known good OBS version" statement since it doesn't depend on OBS version directly, only on obs-websocket being reachable — already satisfied by the installed obs-websocket plugin. |

## Summary of Blocking / Attention Items

1. **Composite Blur and Advanced Masks: must install the `-windows-legacy-x64` build, not the default `-windows-x64` build.** The non-legacy build is for OBS 33+; this environment runs OBS 32.2.2. This was explicitly confirmed in the developer's own v1.6.0 release notes for both plugins (shared build pipeline). Using the wrong asset is the single highest-risk mistake available here.
2. Both plugin ZIP hashes **matched** the SHA256 values published in each GitHub release's notes body — no integrity concern.
3. Composite Blur's zip has an extra top-level `obs-composite-blur\` folder that must be stripped during copy; Advanced Masks' zip does not have this extra folder. Copy logic must account for this difference or files will land one directory level too deep.
4. Streamer.bot has **no official published checksum** — this is a blocking item for anyone requiring hash verification as a hard gate. It is partially mitigated by a valid EV Authenticode signature on `Streamer.bot.exe` (`CN=Streamer.bot`, SSL.com issuer), which at least confirms the binary came from the Streamer.bot organization and hasn't been tampered with post-signing.
5. No open GitHub issues on either FiniteSingularity repo describe a Windows/OBS-32-specific crash or security advisory. A handful of HDR color-handling and mask-interaction bugs are open but not severe/blocking for a standard SDR streaming setup.

async def ensure_downstream_keyer(obs):
    """Make sure the alerts keyer actually points at its scene.

    The Downstream Keyer holds alerts above every scene on channel 7, which
    is why ALR - StreamElements lives in one scene of its own instead of
    being copied into all six. An empty keyer silently renders nothing, and
    the failure looks exactly like a broken alert widget, so assert it on
    every start rather than trusting what is saved in the collection.

    Driven through the plugin's own vendor requests, so the plugin writes
    its config itself and we never have to guess its JSON schema.
    """
    async def vendor(req):
        return await obs.request('CallVendorRequest', {
            "vendorName": "downstream-keyer", "requestType": req,
            "requestData": {"dsk_name": DSK_NAME, "scene": DSK_SCENE}})
    try:
        await vendor('dsk_add_scene')        # no-op if already in the list
        await vendor('dsk_select_scene')     # make it the live layer
        log("downstream keyer '%s' -> '%s'" % (DSK_NAME, DSK_SCENE))

"""
import io, json, os, re, shutil, sys

OBS = os.path.expandvars(r'%APPDATA%\obs-studio')
TOOLS = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))

DROP_SCENE = '2 - Agent Select'

DROP_SOURCES = ['HUD - Season Stats', 'HUD - Valorant Crosshair']
DROP_GROUPS = ['GRP - HUD Agent Select']
RENAME = {
    '3 - Minecraft':    '2 - Minecraft',
    '4 - Starting Soon': '3 - Starting Soon',
    '5 - BRB':          '4 - BRB',
    '6 - Stream Ended':  '5 - Stream Ended',
}
# Final order -> Ctrl+Alt+Fn, so the hotkeys keep matching the numbers.
HOTKEY_ORDER = ['1 - Gaming', '2 - Minecraft', '3 - Starting Soon',
                '4 - BRB', '5 - Stream Ended']


def load(p):
    return json.load(io.open(p, encoding='utf-8'))


def save(p, d, indent=4):
    io.open(p, 'w', encoding='utf-8').write(
        json.dumps(d, indent=indent, ensure_ascii=False))


def migrate_collection(path, say):
    d = load(path)
    names = {s['name'] for s in d['sources']}
    if DROP_SCENE not in names:
        say("collection: %r already gone - nothing to do" % DROP_SCENE)
        return d

    # --- safety: confirm the sources really are exclusive to this scene ---
    doomed = set(DROP_SOURCES) | set(DROP_GROUPS)
    for s in d['sources']:
        if s['id'] != 'scene' or s['name'] == DROP_SCENE:
            continue
        for i in s['settings']['items']:
            if i['name'] in doomed:
                raise SystemExit(
                    "ABORT: %r is also used by %r - not exclusive to %r"
                    % (i['name'], s['name'], DROP_SCENE))

    # --- drop the scene, its group and its two exclusive sources ---
    before = len(d['sources'])
    d['sources'] = [s for s in d['sources']
                    if s['name'] != DROP_SCENE and s['name'] not in doomed]
    say("collection: sources %d -> %d (dropped the scene + %d exclusive)"
        % (before, len(d['sources']), len(doomed)))

    d['groups'] = [g for g in (d.get('groups') or [])
                   if g['name'] not in DROP_GROUPS]
    d['scene_order'] = [o for o in d['scene_order'] if o['name'] != DROP_SCENE]

    # --- renumber: source names, order, and the "current scene" pointers ---
    for s in d['sources']:
        if s['name'] in RENAME:
            s['name'] = RENAME[s['name']]
    for o in d['scene_order']:
        o['name'] = RENAME.get(o['name'], o['name'])
    for key in ('current_scene', 'current_program_scene'):
        cur = d.get(key)
        if cur in RENAME:
            d[key] = RENAME[cur]
        elif cur == DROP_SCENE:
            d[key] = HOTKEY_ORDER[0]      # the dropped scene was live
            say("collection: %s pointed at the dropped scene -> %r"
                % (key, HOTKEY_ORDER[0]))
    say("collection: renumbered %d scenes" % len(RENAME))

    # --- re-seat the scene-select hotkeys as Ctrl+Alt+F1..Fn ---
    pos = {n: i for i, n in enumerate(HOTKEY_ORDER)}
    for s in d['sources']:
        if s['id'] != 'scene' or s['name'] not in pos:
            continue
        hk = s.setdefault('hotkeys', {})
        key = 'OBS_KEY_F%d' % (pos[s['name']] + 1)
        hk['OBSBasic.SelectScene'] = [{"control": True, "alt": True,
                                       "key": key}]
    say("collection: hotkeys -> Ctrl+Alt+F1..F%d in scene order"
        % len(HOTKEY_ORDER))

    # --- nothing may still reference the dropped names ---
    blob = json.dumps(d, ensure_ascii=False)
    for dead in [DROP_SCENE] + list(RENAME) + DROP_SOURCES + DROP_GROUPS:
        if '"%s"' % dead in blob:
            raise SystemExit("ABORT: %r still referenced after migration" % dead)
    return d


def migrate_autopilot_config(path, say):
    c = load(path)
    c['games'] = {k: RENAME.get(v, v) for k, v in c['games'].items()}
    c['managed'] = [RENAME.get(n, n) for n in c['managed']]
    c['gaming_scene'] = RENAME.get(c['gaming_scene'], c['gaming_scene'])
    # With no agent-select scene, agent select is just gameplay.

    c['valorant_managed'] = [RENAME.get(n, n) for n in c['valorant_managed']
                             if n != DROP_SCENE]
    save(path, c, indent=2)
    say("config: managed=%s" % c['managed'])
    say("config: valorant PREGAME -> %r, managed=%s"
        % (c['valorant_scenes']['PREGAME'], c['valorant_managed']))


def migrate_script(path, say):
    s = io.open(path, encoding='utf-8').read()
    orig = s
    s = s.replace('"managed": ["1 - Gaming", "3 - Minecraft"],',

     The port does NOT: it is not a secret, it stays in the source URL, and
     keeping it there means a page never has to guess which port to use.

     This retries instead of falling back, because OBS loads its browser
     sources several seconds BEFORE autopilot binds the HUD server. A
     one-shot fetch loses that race on every cold start, and a fallback
     value would then be wrong for the life of the page - the earlier
     version defaulted to 4455 and hammered a dead port forever. */
  async function resolveConn(opts) {
    if (opts.pw) return { pw: String(opts.pw) };
    for (let wait = 500; ; wait = Math.min(wait * 1.5, 5000)) {
      try {
        const j = await (await fetch('/ws.json', { cache: 'no-store' })).json();
        if (j && j.password) return { pw: String(j.password) };
      } catch (e) { /* HUD server not up yet */ }
      await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, wait));
    }
  }"
  }

input.content:
"""One-shot migration: drop "2 - Agent Select" and close the numbering gap.

Scene names are load-bearing in three places that must move together, which
is why this is a script and not a few clicks:

  Main.json             the scene, scene_order, its hotkey, and the three
                        sources it exclusively owned
  autopilot.config.json every scene name autopilot switches to or guards
  obs-autopilot.py      the same names again, as fallback DEFAULTS

Renumbering is rename-only: the surviving scenes are already in the right
relative order, so scene_order needs the dead entry removed and nothing
resequenced.

  python migrate-drop-agent-select.py --dry-run <dir>   rehearse on a copy
  python migrate-drop-agent-select.py                   apply for real

OBS must be closed when applying: it rewrites the whole collection on exit
and would clobber this.
"""
import io, json, os, re, shutil, sys

OBS = os.path.expandvars(r'%APPDATA%\obs-studio')
TOOLS = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))

DROP_SCENE = '2 - Agent Select'
# Sources only that scene used. Verified against the collection before
# deleting, so a later edit that reuses one of them cannot be silently lost.
DROP_SOURCES = ['HUD - Season Stats', 'HUD - Valorant Crosshair']
DROP_GROUPS = ['GRP - HUD Agent Select']
RENAME = {
    '3 - Minecraft':    '2 - Minecraft',
    '4 - Starting Soon': '3 - Starting Soon',
    '5 - BRB':          '4 - BRB',
    '6 - Stream Ended':  '5 - Stream Ended',
}
# Final order -> Ctrl+Alt+Fn, so the hotkeys keep matching the numbers.
HOTKEY_ORDER = ['1 - Gaming', '2 - Minecraft', '3 - Starting Soon',
                '4 - BRB', '5 - Stream Ended']


def load(p):
    return json.load(io.open(p, encoding='utf-8'))


def save(p, d, indent=4):
    io.open(p, 'w', encoding='utf-8').write(
        json.dumps(d, indent=indent, ensure_ascii=False))


def migrate_collection(path, say):
    d = load(path)
    names = {s['name'] for s in d['sources']}
    if DROP_SCENE not in names:
        say("collection: %r already gone - nothing to do" % DROP_SCENE)
        return d

    # --- safety: confirm the sources really are exclusive to this scene ---
    doomed = set(DROP_SOURCES) | set(DROP_GROUPS)
    for s in d['sources']:
        if s['id'] != 'scene' or s['name'] == DROP_SCENE:
            continue
        for i in s['settings']['items']:
            if i['name'] in doomed:
                raise SystemExit(
                    "ABORT: %r is also used by %r - not exclusive to %r"
                    % (i['name'], s['name'], DROP_SCENE))

    # --- drop the scene, its group and its two exclusive sources ---
    before = len(d['sources'])
    d['sources'] = [s for s in d['sources']
                    if s['name'] != DROP_SCENE and s['name'] not in doomed]
    say("collection: sources %d -> %d (dropped the scene + %d exclusive)"
        % (before, len(d['sources']), len(doomed)))

    d['groups'] = [g for g in (d.get('groups') or [])
                   if g['name'] not in DROP_GROUPS]
    d['scene_order'] = [o for o in d['scene_order'] if o['name'] != DROP_SCENE]

    # --- renumber: source names, order, and the "current scene" pointers ---
    for s in d['sources']:
        if s['name'] in RENAME:
            s['name'] = RENAME[s['name']]
    for o in d['scene_order']:
        o['name'] = RENAME.get(o['name'], o['name'])
    for key in ('current_scene', 'current_program_scene'):
        cur = d.get(key)
        if cur in RENAME:
            d[key] = RENAME[cur]
        elif cur == DROP_SCENE:
            d[key] = HOTKEY_ORDER[0]      # the dropped scene was live
            say("collection: %s pointed at the dropped scene -> %r"
                % (key, HOTKEY_ORDER[0]))
    say("collection: renumbered %d scenes" % len(RENAME))

    # --- re-seat the scene-select hotkeys as Ctrl+Alt+F1..Fn ---
    pos = {n: i for i, n in enumerate(HOTKEY_ORDER)}
    for s in d['sources']:
        if s['id'] != 'scene' or s['name'] not in pos:
            continue
        hk = s.setdefault('hotkeys', {})
        key = 'OBS_KEY_F%d' % (pos[s['name']] + 1)
        hk['OBSBasic.SelectScene'] = [{"control": True, "alt": True,
                                       "key": key}]
    say("collection: hotkeys -> Ctrl+Alt+F1..F%d in scene order"
        % len(HOTKEY_ORDER))

    # --- nothing may still reference the dropped names ---
    blob = json.dumps(d, ensure_ascii=False)
    for dead in [DROP_SCENE] + list(RENAME) + DROP_SOURCES + DROP_GROUPS:
        if '"%s"' % dead in blob:
            raise SystemExit("ABORT: %r still referenced after migration" % dead)
    return d


def migrate_autopilot_config(path, say):
    c = load(path)
    c['games'] = {k: RENAME.get(v, v) for k, v in c['games'].items()}
    c['managed'] = [RENAME.get(n, n) for n in c['managed']]
    c['gaming_scene'] = RENAME.get(c['gaming_scene'], c['gaming_scene'])
    # With no agent-select scene, agent select is just gameplay.
    c['valorant_scenes'] = {k: (c['gaming_scene'] if v == DROP_SCENE
                                else RENAME.get(v, v))
                            for k, v in c['valorant_scenes'].items()}
    c['valorant_managed'] = [RENAME.get(n, n) for n in c['valorant_managed']
                             if n != DROP_SCENE]
    save(path, c, indent=2)
    say("config: managed=%s" % c['managed'])
    say("config: valorant PREGAME -> %r, managed=%s"
        % (c['valorant_scenes']['PREGAME'], c['valorant_managed']))


def migrate_script(path, say):
    s = io.open(path, encoding='utf-8').read()

                  '        "PREGAME": "1 - Gaming",           # agent select\n')
    s = s.replace('"valorant_managed": ["1 - Gaming", "2 - Agent Select"],',
                  '"valorant_managed": ["1 - Gaming"],')
    s = s.replace("('1 - Gaming', '3 - Minecraft')",
                  "('1 - Gaming', '2 - Minecraft')")
    if s == orig:
        say("script: already migrated")
    else:
        io.open(path, 'w', encoding='utf-8', newline='\n').write(s)
        say("script: DEFAULTS + selftest probe updated")
    for dead in [DROP_SCENE] + list(RENAME):
        if dead in s:
            raise SystemExit("ABORT: %r still in %s" % (dead, path))

    n=[0]
    async def req(t,data=None):
        n[0]+=1; rid=str(n[0])
        await ws.send(json.dumps({"op":6,"d":{"requestType":t,"requestId":rid,"requestData":data or {}}}))
        while True:
            m=json.loads(await ws.recv())
            if m.get('op')==7 and m['d']['requestId']==rid:

    items=(await req('GetSceneItemList',{"sceneName":"DSK - Alerts"}))['sceneItems']
    ref=next(i for i in items if i['sourceName']==SRC)
    tr={k:ref['sceneItemTransform'][k] for k in
        ('positionX','positionY','scaleX','scaleY','boundsType','boundsAlignment',
         'boundsWidth','boundsHeight','alignment','rotation')}
    print("reference transform: bounds %sx%s type=%s"%(tr['boundsWidth'],tr['boundsHeight'],tr['boundsType']))

        # top of the stack so alerts are never hidden behind gameplay
        await req('SetSceneItemIndex',{"sceneName":sc,"sceneItemId":iid,
