i < 64; i++) {\n        const s0 = rotr(w[i-15],7) ^ rotr(w[i-15],18) ^ (w[i-15] >>> 3);\n        const s1 = rotr(w[i-2],17) ^ rotr(w[i-2],19) ^ (w[i-2] >>> 10);\n        w[i] = (w[i-16] + s0 + w[i-7] + s1) >>> 0;\n      }\n      let [a,b,c,d,e,f,g,h] = H;\n      for (let i = 0; i < 64; i++) {\n        const S1 = rotr(e,6) ^ rotr(e,11) ^ rotr(e,25);\n        const ch = (e & f) ^ (~e & g);\n        const t1 = (h + S1 + ch + K[i] + w[i]) >>> 0;\n        const S0 = rotr(a,2) ^ rotr(a,13) ^ rotr(a,22);\n        const mj = (a & b) ^ (a & c) ^ (b & c);\n        const t2 = (S0 + mj) >>> 0;\n        h=g; g=f; f=e; e=(d+t1)>>>0; d=c; c=b; b=a; a=(t1+t2)>>>0;\n      }\n      H = H.map((v,i) => (v + [a,b,c,d,e,f,g,h][i]) >>> 0);\n    }\n    const out = [];\n    for (const v of H) out.push((v>>>24)&0xff, (v>>>16)&0xff, (v>>>8)&0xff, v&0xff);\n    return out;\n  }\n  const b64 = a => btoa(String.fromCharCode(...a));\n  const utf8 = s => [...new TextEncoder().encode(s)];\n  const sha256b64 = s => b64(sha256Bytes(utf8(s)));\n\n  function start(opts) {\n    opts = opts || {};\n    const INPUT  = opts.input || 'Desktop Audio';\n    const PORT   = String(opts.port || '4455');\n    const PW     = opts.pw || '';\n    const GAIN   = parseFloat(opts.gain != null ? opts.gain : 1.6);\n    const FLOOR  = parseFloat(opts.floor != null ? opts.floor : -58);\n    const target = opts.target || document.documentElement;\n    const onLevel = opts.onLevel;\n\n    /* ---- fast attack so transients pop, slow release ---- */\n    let level = 0, peak = 0;\n    function paint() {\n      level += (peak - level) * (peak > level ? 0.55 : 0.12);\n      const v = Math.max(0, Math.min(1, level));\n      target.style.setProperty('--glow', v.toFixed(3));\n      if (onLevel) onLevel(v);\n      requestAnimationFrame(paint);\n    }\n    target.style.setProperty('--glow', '0');\n    requestAnimationFrame(paint);\n\n    let ws, retry = 0;\n    function connect() {\n      try { ws = new WebSocket('ws://127.0.0.1:' + PORT); options.label: Twitch only
options.description: I write a direct Twitch IRC-over-websocket client. Needs only your channel name, no login, and gives full control over styling, badges and emotes.

options.label: YouTube only
options.description: YouTube live chat has no open socket; it needs either the Data API (API key + live video ID) or a third-party relay.

options.label: Twitch + YouTube
options.description: Both feeds merged into one list with a small platform marker per message. More moving parts, and YouTube still needs an API key.

options.label: Wrap an existing widget
options.description: Embed the StreamElements/Streamlabs chat widget inside the chrome frame. Fastest, but styling is limited to what their widget exposes and it needs your login.

questions.question: How should messages behave in the box?

options.label: Scroll up, keep history
options.description: Classic chat: newest at the bottom, older messages scroll up and stay until they run off the top of the 400x600 box.

options.label: Fade out after a while
options.description: Messages appear, hold for ~30s, then fade away so the box self-clears during quiet moments. Good for an on-stream overlay.

options.label: Newest at top

import glob, io, re
# Sweep every colour literal in every overlay and flag any that reads cool,
# i.e. blue channel dominant, or green dominant over red.
hexes = re.compile(r'#([0-9a-fA-F]{6}|[0-9a-fA-F]{3})\b')
rgba  = re.compile(r'rgba?\(\s*(\d+)\s*,\s*(\d+)\s*,\s*(\d+)')
bad = 0
for fn in sorted(glob.glob('*.html') + glob.glob('*.css')):
    txt = io.open(fn, encoding='utf-8').read()
    for ln, line in enumerate(txt.splitlines(), 1):
        if line.strip().startswith('*') or '//' in line.split('#')[0][:4]: pass
        for m in hexes.finditer(line):
            h = m.group(1)
            if len(h) == 3: h = ''.join(c*2 for c in h)
            r, g, b = int(h[0:2],16), int(h[2:4],16), int(h[4:6],16)
            if max(r,g,b) < 18: continue          # near-black is neutral
            if b > r or (g > r + 6):
                print("  COOL %-16s:%-4d #%s  rgb(%d,%d,%d)" % (fn, ln, h, r,g,b)); bad += 1
        for m in rgba.finditer(line):
            r,g,b = (int(x) for x in m.groups())
            if max(r,g,b) < 18 or r==g==b: continue   # black / true neutral
            if b > r or (g > r + 6):
                print("  COOL %-16s:%-4d rgb(%d,%d,%d)" % (fn, ln, r,g,b)); bad += 1

async def scene_switcher(obs, cfg, stop):
    """Follow the foreground game, but never fight a manual scene choice.

    The old version only acted when the foreground exe *changed*, which
    sounds like enough but is not: alt-tabbing out of a game and back in
    counts as a change, so it re-fired and yanked the streamer off a scene
    they had just picked by hotkey. With a second game left running in the
    background that happened constantly.

    So manual control now wins. The moment the program scene is something
    autopilot did not set, it backs off and stays off until the foreground
    game actually becomes a *different* game - at which point following
    again is clearly what the streamer wants.
    """
    games = {k.lower(): v for k, v in cfg['games'].items()}
    managed = set(cfg['managed'])
    applied = None        # the scene autopilot itself last set
    held_for = None       # exe in front when the streamer took over
    while not stop.is_set():
        try:
            exe = foreground_exe()
            key = (exe or '').lower()
            target = games.get(key) or cfg.get('fallback_scene')
            cur = obs.current_scene or await obs.scene()

            # Someone moved the scene behind our back -> that is a manual
            # override. Record which game was in front so we know when the
            # situation has genuinely changed.
            if cur != applied and cur != target and applied is not None:
                if held_for != key:
                    log("manual scene '%s' - autopilot holding until the game changes" % cur)
                held_for = key
            # a different game in front clears the hold
            elif held_for is not None and held_for != key:
                held_for = None

            if target and target != cur:
                if held_for == key:
                    pass                      # streamer is driving
                elif cur in managed:
                    await obs.set_scene(target)
                    applied = target
                    log("%s -> scene '%s'" % (exe, target))
                else:
                    log("%s wants '%s' but holding on '%s' (not managed)"
                        % (exe, target, cur))
        except Exception as e:
            log("switcher: %s" % e)
        await asyncio.sleep(cfg['switch_poll_seconds'])

Groups are the right tool here — a nested scene would come out canvas-sized and need cropping, whereas a group sizes itself to its children. OBS's websocket API can't create groups, so this is an offline edit.

Flipping the order and widening the gap. Cleanest to rebuild from the pre-pair backup rather than patch the group I just made.

Loaded cleanly — **0 duplicates, 0 id collisions**. Let me confirm it looks right.

Done — cam on top, keyboard and mouse below, 20px gap, all in one group.

**`Cam + Inputs` — 270×258**, a single element you can drag and scale as a unit:

```
 y   0..152   cam  (frame 270×152, handcam inset 257×145)
 y 152..172   20px gap
 y 172..258   keyboard 202×86 + mouse 57×85
```

Placed in all five scenes with a cam, every one at a 15px margin:

| Scene | Position |
|---|---|
| 1 - Valorant | (15, 15) |
| 2 - Agent Select | (15, 15) |
| 3 - The Finals | (15, 807) |
| 4 - Gameplay | (1635, 549) |
| 6 - Minecraft | (1635, 549) |

**Verified on a cold load: 0 duplicate renders, 0 id collisions** — the two failure modes that bit me on previous hand-built groups. The old `Cam Module (Valorant)`, `Cam Module (Finals)`, `Cam Module (General)` and `Input Module` groups are gone, replaced by this one; four groups became one.

Two details worth knowing:

- **Child order matters and I set it deliberately**: handcam renders *below* the frame so the border sits over the cam's edge, matching how the old Cam Module was layered. My first attempt had it inverted — I'd have had the handcam covering its own frame.
- **One frame for all games now.** A group has one set of children, so the per-game frame variants (`Frame Valorant` / `Frame Finals` / `Frame General`) can't coexist in a single element — it uses `Cam - Frame General` everywhere. Since the colour sweep brought all three into the same amber range, they were nearly identical anyway, but you do lose the per-game accent tint. If you want it back, the options are three paired variants or driving the frame's accent from autopilot per scene — say the word.

I rebuilt this from the `.pre-pair` backup rather than patching the version I'd already written with the inputs on top, so there's no leftover from that first pass. Rollback if needed: `Main.json.pre-pair`.

```json
# a child entry as it lives inside the group (local coordinates)
```

    z = zipfile.ZipFile(zf); n = 0
    # the dll

    n += 1

    for i in z.infolist():
        if i.is_dir() or not i.filename.startswith(data_prefix): continue
        if i.filename.endswith('.pdb'): continue
        rel = i.filename[len(data_prefix):]
        d2 = os.path.join(OBS, "data", "obs-plugins", data_name, rel.replace('/', os.sep))

            shutil.copyfileobj(f, out)

instruction: do i need kiwix for this or for rag retrievals?
output:
Short answer: **no.** Let me confirm it concretely rather than assert it:

Confirmed: **Kiwix is not installed on your machine**, and the ZIM retrieval we tested earlier worked anyway.

## Why you don't need it

ZIM is an open format, and `libzim` is the official reader library — `libzim.pyd`, the single dependency, already installed. Everything else `zimrag.py` imports is standard library (`html`, `re`, `pathlib`, `dataclasses`, `functools`, `unicodedata`).

Kiwix (the desktop app / `kiwix-serve`) is just *one consumer* of ZIM files. It happens to be the most famous one, so the format gets called "Kiwix files", but the reader and the format are separate things. The Xapian full-text index that makes our search instant is baked into the `.zim` file itself by the scraper — not provided by Kiwix.

| | needs Kiwix? |
|---|---|
| search across archives | no — `libzim.search.Searcher` |
| extract article text | no — `libzim.reader.Archive` |
| RAG with citations | no |
| the built-in full-text index | no — it's inside the file |

## Where Kiwix *would* earn its place

Two cases, one of which applies directly to you:

1. **Reading as a human** — browsing articles with images, formatting and links. `zimrag` returns plain text to a model; it's not a reading experience.
2. **The 204 GB of video you're downloading.** This is the real one. Khan Academy (180 GB) and TED (24 GB) are mostly video payload — `zimrag` can only index their sparse text, and it certainly can't play a lecture. If you want any value from those two archives, you need Kiwix (or another ZIM reader with a media player). Without it, that 204 GB is effectively inert.

So for the retrieval pipeline: not needed, nothing to install. For the media archives you chose to include: install `kiwix-desktop` and point it at `E:\LocalLLM\zims` — it reads the same directory, so both tools share one corpus with no duplication.

If you want it, `winget install Kiwix.Kiwix` is the usual route on Windows; `kiwix-serve` is the headless variant if you'd rather browse the corpus over HTTP from other devices on your network. Say the word and I'll set either up — but the RAG side is complete without it.

instruction: do i need kiwix for this or for rag retrievals?
output:
Short answer: **no.** Let me confirm it concretely rather than assert it:

Confirmed: **Kiwix is not installed on your machine**, and the ZIM retrieval we tested earlier worked anyway.

## Why you don't need it

ZIM is an open format, and `libzim` is the official reader library — `libzim.pyd`, the single dependency, already installed. Everything else `zimrag.py` imports is standard library (`html`, `re`, `pathlib`, `dataclasses`, `functools`, `unicodedata`).

Kiwix (the desktop app / `kiwix-serve`) is just *one consumer* of ZIM files. It happens to be the most famous one, so the format gets called "Kiwix files", but the reader and the format are separate things. The Xapian full-text index that makes our search instant is baked into the `.zim` file itself by the scraper — not provided by Kiwix.

| | needs Kiwix? |
|---|---|
| search across archives | no — `libzim.search.Searcher` |
| extract article text | no — `libzim.reader.Archive` |
| RAG with citations | no |
| the built-in full-text index | no — it's inside the file |

## Where Kiwix *would* earn its place

Two cases, one of which applies directly to you:

1. **Reading as a human** — browsing articles with images, formatting and links. `zimrag` returns plain text to a model; it's not a reading experience.
2. **The 204 GB of video you're downloading.** This is the real one. Khan Academy (180 GB) and TED (24 GB) are mostly video payload — `zimrag` can only index their sparse text, and it certainly can't play a lecture. If you want any value from those two archives, you need Kiwix (or another ZIM reader with a media player). Without it, that 204 GB is effectively inert.

So for the retrieval pipeline: not needed, nothing to install. For the media archives you chose to include: install `kiwix-desktop` and point it at `E:\LocalLLM\zims` — it reads the same directory, so both tools share one corpus with no duplication.

If you want it, `winget install Kiwix.Kiwix` is the usual route on Windows; `kiwix-serve` is the headless variant if you'd rather browse the corpus over HTTP from other devices on your network. Say the word and I'll set either up — but the RAG side is complete without it.

```json
  "input": {
    "command": "cd \"C:/Users/Srini\" && echo \"=== is kiwix installed anywhere? ===\"; which kiwix kiwix-serve kiwix-desktop 2>/dev/null || echo \"(no kiwix binaries on PATH)\"; powershell -Command \"Get-ChildItem 'C:\\Program Files','C:\\Program Files (x86)','$env:LOCALAPPDATA\\Programs' -Filter '*iwix*' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object -First 3 -ExpandProperty Name\" 2>&1 | tail -3; echo \"=== what zimrag actually depends on ===\"; python -c \"\nimport libzim, sys\nprint('libzim:', libzim.__file__)\nprint('python:', sys.version.split()[0])\n\"; grep -hoE \"^(import|from) [a-z_]+\" \"E:/LocalLLM/zimrag/zimrag.py\" | sort -u | tr '\\n' ' '",
    "description": "Verify Kiwix is absent and list real dependencies",
    "timeout": 180000
  }
}
```

instruction: one question, if i train my local models and then pull newer versions if any what happens to the trained data?
output:
Good question, and the answer splits three ways. Let me check what your adapters are actually pinned to:

Three separate things, three different fates. (I also see you're up to `lesson_15` now — 3.8 GB of adapters.)

## 1. Your training data and adapters are physically safe

`ollama pull` only writes to `E:\LocalLLM\models` (the Ollama blob store, 32 GB). It never touches:

- `dataset/*.jsonl` — your actual training data
- `adapters/lesson_01..15/` — 3.8 GB of trained weights
- `adapters/lesson_ledger.json`

**There are two entirely separate weight stores on this machine**, and that's what protects you:

| store | size | used for | affected by `ollama pull`? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `E:\LocalLLM\models` | 32 GB | GGUF, inference | yes |
| `~/.cache/huggingface` (WSL) | 8.8 GB | safetensors, training base | **no** |

Training reads the second; Ollama writes the first. They don't intersect.

## 2. But the adapters are pinned to exact base weights — this is the real risk

Every one of your adapters records `base_model_name_or_path = unsloth/Qwen3.5-4B`, `r=16`, `alpha=32`. A LoRA is a **delta against specific weights**, not a standalone model, so it's only meaningful against the weights it was trained on.

| what you pull | what happens to the adapters |
|---|---|
| A **different model** (Qwen3.8, Gemma 4, Granite) | Won't load — different dimensions. Nothing is lost, but nothing transfers either; you'd retrain |
| A **new revision of the same model** (unsloth re-uploads Qwen3.5-4B) | **The dangerous case.** Shapes still match, so it loads fine — but the deltas no longer correspond to those weights, and quality degrades *silently*. Nothing errors |

That second row is the one to guard against. And note it's triggered by the **HF cache** being replaced, not by `ollama pull` — your adapters are indifferent to Ollama entirely.

## 3. What `ollama pull` does destroy today

The baked-in operator profile. Pulling `qwen3.5:9b` replaces the manifest and the SYSTEM block goes with it. One command restores it:

```powershell
python E:\LocalLLM\profile\build_persona_models.py --model 4b --model 9b --model granite3b --model granite8b --model gemma2b --model nemotron
```

## 4. What's immune to everything

```
gguf/student_v1-f16.gguf    8.42 GB
gguf/student_v1-q8_0.gguf   4.48 GB
```

These are **merged** — base and adapter already fused into one file. No dependency on any base, any cache, or any registry. They survive any pull. (They're still the ones Ollama can't load because of the `ssm_beta_alpha` layout mismatch, but as artifacts they're self-contained and portable.)

## The practical takeaway

**Your dataset is the durable asset, not the adapters.** Lesson 5 trained 745 examples in 365 seconds — adapters are cheap to regenerate, data isn't. Back up `dataset/*.jsonl` and `lesson_ledger.json`; treat `adapters/` as a cache.

Two things I'd add if you want them:
1. **Pin the base revision** in `train_student.py` and record it in the ledger, so a silent upstream re-upload can't quietly invalidate 15 lessons' worth of work — and so you can reproduce exactly.
2. **A `--verify-base` check** that compares the current HF cache digest against what the ledger says each adapter trained on, and warns loudly on mismatch.

The second one specifically closes the silent-degradation hole. Say the word and I'll build both.

```json
    "command": "cd \"E:/LocalLLM/teacher_pipeline\" && python -c \"\nimport json\nfrom pathlib import Path\nfor d in sorted(Path('adapters').glob('lesson_0*')):\n    cfg = d/'adapter_config.json'\n    if cfg.exists():\n        c = json.loads(cfg.read_text(encoding='utf-8'))\n        print(f\\\"{d.name}: base={c.get('base_model_name_or_path')} r={c.get('r')} alpha={c.get('lora_alpha')}\\\")\n\" 2>&1 | head -6; echo \"=== merged standalone exports ===\"; ls -la gguf/*.gguf 2>/dev/null | awk '{printf \\\"%.2f GB  %s\\n\\\", $5/1e9, $9}'; echo \"=== the two separate weight stores ===\"; du -sh \"E:/LocalLLM/models\" 2>/dev/null | sed 's/$/   <- Ollama (inference)/'; wsl -d Ubuntu -- bash -lc 'du -sh ~/.cache/huggingface 2>/dev/null' | sed 's/$/   <- HF cache in WSL (training base)/'",
```
